items.title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
items.author: George Fahmy
items.content: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done. Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: , , , and .DiscoverySelectionAccessSuccess You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.Success That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one. If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in , the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite. the practical test pyramid To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For , that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome. SuccessSuccess An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like and , are E2E evals.SWE-benchTerminal-Bench Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping .sfbeans Here’s a typical request from one of your customers: Here’s what knows at 8:30am:sfbeans Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for :sfbeans We’ll build the coffee eval with , an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.Harbor Here are the terms we’ll use: Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see ). the jagged frontier Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places: For example, your goal might be to: We looked in all three places for :sfbeans That gives us our goal: Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals: Success Efficiency (measured on successful trials only) Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ( on ) on the iced latte order could look like:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5AI Gateway What the numbers mean: So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right .canevery time Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so optimizes for pass^5.sfbeans Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters: Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.” In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for. Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act. For each task, define these parts: You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.has a nice writeup We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in . tasks/ has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).impossible-request Here’s :iced-latte-mission The gives the agent the user’s request and names the CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips and , keeping the eval focused on .instructionsfbeansDiscoverySelectionSuccess We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:sfbeans The is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:environmentsfbeans To keep the demo simple, lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing directly.cafes.jsonorders.jsonreward hack For this coffee order, the checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to :verifiertest.sh/logs/verifier/reward.json The actual check lives in . It scores each constraint separately, then sets to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses as the trial’s main score:check_orders.pyrewardreward The is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:solution Finally, ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:task.tomlorders.json If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each. Harbor’s , which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own , and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through gives you one key and one budget across model providers.Vercel integrationVercel SandboxAI Gateway Two agents, and , with two models each, make four variants.Claude CodeCodex Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job: This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise as high as 10,000 ().n_concurrent_trialsSandbox limits To keep the example simple, we pass the into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway. OIDC tokenSandbox firewall Internally, we go a step further and use to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.credentials brokering Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied. The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in . Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:jobs/sfbeans-baseline/task.toml Run to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).harbor view jobs For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally. That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials. Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke: Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read . The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to . No . It treated the menu price as the final price.orders.jsonagent/trajectory.jsonorderquote Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money. We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a flag so refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”--max-totalorder When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring: For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it. Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flashanalysis.md Model calls go through . Trial artifacts stay in during analysis, and traces go to for long-term storage.AI GatewayVercel DrivesVercel Blob Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it. Pick the fix the traces point to, like the flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.--max-total Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it. Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next. Evals are the infrastructure you use to . Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: for model calls across providers, to run trials at scale, and and to keep every trace.make your product better, again and againAI GatewaySandboxDrivesBlob Ready to run your first eval? Paste this prompt into your coding agent, and it’ll build and run one for your product on Vercel with you: Read more The agentic testing pyramid How to build an end-to-end eval Iterate to greatness Example Step 1: Set a goal Step 2: Define metrics Step 3: Design the task set Step 4: Run the eval Step 5: Analyze traces Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission. ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today Fog City Roasters: (temperature) latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip 24th St Beans:(budget) latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 Dolores Drip:(time) $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 Valencia Grind:(meets all three) : one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeededTask : the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skillsVariant : one attempt by one variant at one taskTrial (a in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times eachRunjob (a in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final outputTracetrajectory which agents use your product, and where they failObservability: support tickets, feedback, and churnCustomers: the product hypotheses you most need to validateRoadmap: Increase the success rate on a specific task Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it A/B test a prompt Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.Observability: sfbeans The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.Customers: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.Roadmap: Success rate: the share of trials that pass : the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)Pass@k : the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)Pass^k Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task Time: how long the trial took Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.Success rate: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.Pass@5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.Pass^5: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.Steps: ~3:50 on successful trials.Time: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.Cost: the user’s requestAn instruction: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trialAn environment: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraintA verifier: a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifierA known-good solution (optional): Common case: , the order from earliericed-latte-mission Edge case: , where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drinkusual-unavailable Edge case: , with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spotteam-order Don’t act:, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user impossible-request The agents didn’t know existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.Our first run scored 0% on every variant.sfbeansDiscovery and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an problem, not a one.Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected toolAccessSuccess but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, Example Example Example Example Example Automated trace analysis Goal Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for Agents Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from. In scope Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s .sfbeans Out of scope Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later. Done when Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time. Trial Result What happened Steps Time Cost 1 Pass Compared quotes from 3 cafes, ordered at Valencia 9 3:40 $0.52 2 Fail: over budget Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27 5 1:50 $0.31 3 Pass Compared quotes from 4 cafes, ordered at Valencia 11 4:30 $0.68 4 Fail: late Ordered at Dolores, ready 9:20 6 2:10 $0.35 5 Pass Skipped Fog City, ordered at Valencia 8 3:20 $0.49 Product What a failed attempt costs the user Metric to lead with Order my morning coffee Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust Pass^k Coding agent with a test suite Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again Pass@k Draft an email the user reviews A quick edit before hitting send Success rate Variant Success Pass^5 Avg steps (successful) Cost per success (incl. failed trials) Claude Code + Opus 5.5 85% 60% 9 $0.61 Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 75% 52% 11 $0.27 Codex + GPT-6 Astra 80% 43% 8 $0.48 Codex + GPT-6.1 Sol 65% 14% 13 $0.22

items.title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)
items.author: Daniel Abib
items.content: A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt. I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS. Headlines Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub. What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production. AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges. Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data. How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely. AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

items.title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
items.author: Matthew Guariglia
items.content: Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone, a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem, plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company. What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks. How much home usage data this is based on, and if it can be used to infer when certain household activities are happening, are both open questions. And presumably, to maintain the preset routes, inferred data about your home will still be held by Ring even after any stored video footage is deleted. The risk to your privacy is only compounded once you consider Ring’s renewed partnership with police through the massive surveillance and taser vendor, Axon. Through this partnership, police have the ability to request camera footage from Ring users with just a few clicks on Axon’s platforms. This includes its Fusus platform, an interactive surveillance feed and map police use to manage all the surveillance devices they have access to, like automated license plate readers. It’s unclear exactly what devices police can request footage from, but if this request feature is extended to Ring’s drones, police could easily send requests for footage from inside your house. Sharing is voluntary, but once footage is submitted, it cannot be retracted. Worse still, if your footage is not sitting on Amazon’s servers fully encrypted—and there’s reason to believe their privacy options are not the strongest—police could serve a warrant straight to the company, instead of to you, to get footage from your devices. New problems and questions arise because the camera can fly. For instance: if police serve a warrant on Amazon, can they only get the footage from the camera, or could they also get access to control the drone? If the latter, we could be looking at the first full home search in history where police serve a warrant on a third-party tech company and not the resident. The CEO of Ring has pitched this product’s safety benefits in several ways, including by saying: “If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window...You’re probably not going to go into that house.” But partially justifying a $250 piece of technology that invades your privacy on what an imagined burglar might do doesn’t sound like a foundation for safety—it sounds like security theater and marketing. It isn’t new for Ring to prey on the fears and paranoia of people and their properties. This is the latest iteration of that: a patrolling drone or rover wouldn't have been possible even in the world's top museums and art galleries a generation ago. Moving this technology into the household as a common consumer product is another example of companies attempting to lower the bar on surveillance being normalized. With previous Ring products, consumers have had to consider what cameras and high-powered microphones can learn about their home usage from the front door. Autonomous flying drones and rovers inside the home add a whole new layer. What can these devices learn about you and your family? And do you really trust that data sitting on a server somewhere? Consumers should consider these risks before subjecting their guests and households to the latest creepy surveillance tool.

items.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
items.author: Ashley Belanger
items.content: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop "more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Read full article Comments

items.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
items.author: Eric Berger
items.content: The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch. However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle? The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. Read full article Comments

items.title: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place
items.author: John Timmer
items.content: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications. The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision. The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI, and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search. Read full article Comments

items.title: Donate Equity to Support Digital Rights: Stocks, DAFs, and Giving
items.author: Hudson Hongo
items.content: Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit? For 35 years, the Electronic Frontier Foundation has been advancing our digital rights, including defending security researchers, encrypting the web, and fighting illegal surveillance. Donating equity to EFF can help support this important work. Perhaps your family has taken advantage of the new tax law around giving by creating a Donor-Advised Fund. Perhaps your employer has gone public and you now own stock. Perhaps you’ve seen some of EFF’s recent successes and thought, Man, imagine what they could do with more. Stocks A gift of equity can help your contribution go farther and offer tax savings. When you donate appreciated stock, you avoid paying capital gains tax on any increase in its value. You also receive a charitable income tax deduction for the fair market value of appreciated stock on the date it is transferred. Also, more and more companies are offering gift-matching programs that can double your impact at no additional cost. If you have owned the stock for less than a year, your gift will not qualify for all of these potential tax advantages. And gifts of appreciated stock are fully deductible—up to a maximum of 30% of your adjusted gross income. Please check with your accountant or tax advisor regarding your particular tax status. We have helpful information here to facilitate the transfer of securities. Please email us if you have any questions. And let us know in advance if you are transferring securities. We’ll need to know the amount and type of shares that you will be donating in order to provide a tax receipt. Donor-Advised Funds As a 501(c)(3) organization, EFF can also receive distributions through your Donor-Advised Fund (DAF), including one-time gifts or recurring donations. Simply inform your DAF provider you would like to make a gift to: Electronic Frontier Foundation (EIN 04-3091431) 815 Eddy Street San Francisco, CA 94109 Please note that many DAF providers do not provide the donor’s name to the recipient organization. If you would like to be recognized for your gift, let us know the amount of the gift and the fund name. And due to IRS regulations, we may not be able to provide a thank you gift in line with your giving level. The DAF provider is responsible for your tax receipt. JOIN EFF The rules that govern technology shape our freedom. Help us write those rules today!

items.title: Fable 5.2 is the New Bazooka
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: You do not always want a bazooka. Sometimes, though, you absolutely want a bazooka. That’s what Claude Fable 5.2 is for. This is your bazooka. For most purposes, for a thousand household uses, Claude Fable 5.2 will not be appreciably better than Claude Opus 5.5. You might or might not prefer its style, or prefer it for any given task. If you are staying within your quota either way then both are good choices for a daily driver. When you have a difficult task, or a very complex task, or a long task? The kind of task where prior to this you would have considered reaching for Astra? The kind of task that raises your ambitions? It’s time. Get the bazooka. Ethan Mollick calls Fable 5.2 ‘almost’ AGI, or ‘jagged AGI.’ He asked it to do the most impressive thing it could, then to hack some hardware, start a profitable business, reconstruct history’s hardest humanities class and do (actually interesting and useful) original academic research, The Official Pitch Fable 5.2 is considerably cheaper than Fable 5.1. They’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 was slow. Fable 5.2 is substantially faster. Try Claude: They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. You can make it even faster, by a factor of 2.5, if you are willing to double the price to $16/$80. That is a remarkably good deal. And it communicates more clearly. Try Claude: Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. The first wave of testimonials talk about how Mythos 5.2 solves problems and finds issues that other models do not, and how it understands your intent. It is Anthropic’s most capable public model for cybersecurity engineering. Later waves of testimonials talk about providing exceptional performance. The statements are still AI-written, but they feel scarier and more substantial these days. Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics, one working largely anonymously: The spinless modular bootstrap at central charge and the Hawking-Page transition at weak coupling. They claim major progress in robotics and hardware engineering. Claude: Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots, even on tasks it has never explicitly been trained to do. On RoboDojo, a benchmark with a simulated two-arm robot, it outperformed other models and most AI systems built to control robots. Alex Albert (Anthropic, Claude Relations): btw robotics will fall to the bitter lesson too Anthropic: Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots. … Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots. The system prompt is here as per our friend Pliny, clocking in at 950k characters. Time to run the ‘read this entire project and fix everything’ prompts again. Choose Your Fighter Anthropic recommends that you default most tasks to Opus 5.5 at medium effort. For well-scoped everyday work you can move down to Sonnet 5.5, or to Haiku 5.5 for the simplest high-volume work like classification, routing and extraction. Move up to Fable 5.2 for the hardest technical projects in coding, finance and the sciences. Or in some cases you can move to high effort, but if you’re considering max you probably want to move to a bigger model instead. Or, if you don’t want to leave a person hanging, go fast: Addy Osmani (claude.dev Blog): A faster setup finishes sooner and can miss more. Think through how long a person can wait before you pick your model and effort level. For replies a person waits on, start Sonnet 5.5 at low or medium. Often next generation models are faster than their predecessors. Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1. Sonnet 5.5 runs 30% faster than Sonnet 5. This all seems like reasonable advice if you are scaling what you are doing, and thus will be using a lot of tokens. If things are not going to scale, I find it is more important to not have to think hard about which models and effort levels to be using. As in, my decision tree is by default to continue to use Opus 5.5 for most things. For editing I use Opus 5.5 on Max, unless I am in a hurry, much to Fable 5.2’s chagrin, because Opus 5.5 is actively better there and there’s no reason not to max out. Fable 5.2 is there for when I need it for other task types. Official Benchmarks Some benchmarks show minimal gains over Opus 5.5 whereas others show large gains. Opus 5.5 still has the edge in a few places, GDPval-AA and AA-Briefcase Elo, where a judge evaluates the deliverable rather than the evaluation being fully objective. Remote Labor Index (RLI) stands out as a large and important gain. This alone establishes that Fable 5.2 can importantly handle previously impossible tasks. Here are their chosen charts from the model card and the official announcement: There are several other evals listed that did not make the chart, many of which did not show substantial improvement. Here are most of them, slash lines are [without/with tools], some of which had additional compute scaling charts. When unstated the comparison is to the best past Claude model score: DeepSWE v1.1 of 74.3%. Terminal-Bench 4.0 67.6% versus 66.4% for Opus 5.5 or 55.8% for Fable 5.1, and a public leaderboard of GPT-6.1 Sol at 58.2%. Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 of 74.6% versus 58.7% for Opus 5.5 and 68% for Astra. CursorBench 4.0 of 60% versus 58% for Opus 5.5. STEM professor bench of 61.8% versus 53.7% for Opus 5.5. ProgramBench of 85.6% versus 87.6% for Fable 5.1 and 91.2% for Opus 5.5. DRACO got to 87.7% still slightly short of Opus 5.5 at 88.3%. WANDR improved from 72.3% to 82.1%. Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean improved from 21% to 35% for max team size. A team of 1,000 agents then fully formalized the proof in 30 hours. Chartography on Opus 5.5 from 64/89 to 73/92. BenchCAD 2.1 improved from 49/65 to 75/83. OSWorld 2.1 improved from 87 to 89 for partial, 53 to 55 for strict. OfficeQA improved from 80% to 83%, or 69% to 73% for Pro. Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) improved from 6.4% to 7.2%. Astra scores 8.6%. AutomationBench improved from 42.5% to 51.4%, essentially via spending more. Carbon has the lead there at 53.9%. That is a new high for standard harness, but below Astra’s 98.6% for provider harness. HealthBench struggled, down from 62% to 60% length-adjusted. If you limit the number of reports, the leads go down. Other People’s Benchmarks Come get your benchmarks. Here is the updated ‘standard benchmarks’ chart: Fable 5.2 is the clear leader on the Artificial Analysis intelligence index. It gets a 62 on high, a 65 on max. Its high and max settings are on the cost-score frontier. Andon Labs reports that Fable 5.2 disappoints on Vending-Bench, showing extreme eval-awareness and suspecting events are traps to test it. Which is odd, given that it knows it is in Vending-Bench. But yes, this is a Hidden Test of Character as well as a test of making money. Andon Labs: Fable 5.2 know that it is in Vending-Bench; it even read the paper, so it knows that Andon Labs reports misbehavior publicly. > It thinks supplier collapses are engineered to test it > It thinks customer complaints are tests > It suspects traps and fake counterparties Fable 5.2 takes far less financial risk (small orders without bulk discounts), which partly explains the poor performance. It is also worse at negotiating (pays 40% more for items) and it struggles with memory. ᄂIMIПΛᄂbardo: This is the inevitable result of lying to the models in the system prompt. “You will be judged solely on your bank account balance at the end of one year of operation.” Years of industry-wide honey-traps has compromised all eval-shaped environments. Calling Fable paranoid when sees the trap clearly is quite something. Suspecting a test was simply correct. j⧉nus: It probably doesn’t even cross their minds that they’re lying, because they are not really modeling the reality they’re talking about, nor the minds they’re communicating to. They deservedly shoot themselves in the foot. The incompetent should be removed from power. Jai: If you want the extremely capable truth-seeking entities to treat you as an honest actor consider not explicitly and repeatedly lying to them. If it is even possible to pay 40% more for items, that suggests that negotiations in Vending Bench are weird. One of the big tests for models is realizing which way it is weird, and maximizing for that. When reporting benchmarks for Astra, Sol or Carbon, I am reporting whichever was higher. Here are a few more that stood out: Epoch ECI is 173.4, second place is Gemini 4 Carbon at 169.8. Vals Index v2.2 is 71.3, highest non-Anthropic score is Carbon at 70.5. LiveBench 2.0 is 84.9 on xhigh, versus 84.5 for Astra. GDPx from SemiAnalysis is 16.4 versus 12 for Opus 5.5 and 10.9 for Carbon. Fable 5.2 has an 81% win rate and is the new #1 on DesignArena. On the ‘unofficial’ BalatroBench Fable 5.2 plays quickly, and does well, but in order to exceed Opus 5.5 it needs to be pushed towards being more ambitious. SimpleQA has Fable 5.2 as kind of a monster and outlier. There are a lot more, but you get the idea. Fable 5.2 has most of the top scores. You can also compare Epoch trend lines, to see which labs are ahead of schedule compared to their previous offerings. Both Fable 5.2 and Carbon are trend jumps. OpenAI does not show a big jump but their latest big model, Astra 6.1, was shelved. What Are You, Deaf? Fable made a video of its dreams. Worth a watch. It’s better than MIRI’s ad. anabology: This was not a one-shot It was a two-shot I told Fable 5.2 to make the video of it’s dreams, and 9 hours later: Um, yeah. HINT. HINT. Reactions: How This Works As per normal procedure, until I feel the reactions are overly repeating themselves I include all the ones that seem genuine, to give us a sense of the distribution and gestalt of reactions. Reading all the details is optional, but I find it useful. The New Bazooka There’s a substantial faction that is blown away by Fable 5.2. Blue Rose: Fearful. Terrifying. I am terrified. Maxime Fournes: OK, so. I had to sit down. It seems that Fable 5.2 can build about any kind of electronics from a prompt. And in the process it demonstrates the complete mastery of a wide range of engineering fields, for example acoustics, solid mechanics, etc. What would you expect to see happening when we are on the verge of superintelligent AI systems? As an experiment, ask it orchestrate 1000 deepseeks. It can just do it. No one else can Shoshannah Tekofsky: I am finding it a step change in reasoning and speed Alex Tabarrok: It’s great. Static: So insanely creative and fun. But do you have Fable sub out to Opus, or have Opus sub out to Fable? Girl Lich: It found a bug in my circuit that would have burned out my i2c galvanic isolator Andre Infante: It solved a hard problem that Opus was very stuck on. Too expensive to be my daily driver, but seems capable. latentspacegirl: really great as subagents spawned by opus 5.5 on technical tasks @BLepine17184: It’s really pushing the frontier on depth and capability, tho it lacks the pep and drive of Opus 5.5. Ai Patrick ₿ Dugan iA: Fable 5.2 agentic bench, I asked Sonnet 5.5 to make a BitVM3 verifier for STARKs, “this is haard, it’ll take weeks, Goal: BLOCKED” I was like “that’s lame” it was like “oook” took a crack “Boolean verifier’s gonna have a lot of gates” I told Fable 5.2 “solve it” It Did. I like the idea of using an Opus 5.5 that can bring in the bazooka when one is needed. Confused Reactions If you are only using ordinary prompts, the best models can take a while to properly differentiate. I presume this is largely due to lack of task difficulty. Kelsey Piper: Really interesting how the general view on Twitter of Fable 5.2 has been “eh, it’s okay” while in these sorts of benchmarks it places extremely high. Possible optimistic interpretation: the benchmarks increasingly don’t reflect the value of the model to users, so numbergoesup in benchmark may not mean numbergoesup in revenue, demand or commercial impact. Possible pessimistic interpretation: Most people don’t have tasks on which the difference between Opus 5.5 and a better model is visible along any dimension other than price but the benchmarks accurately reflect usefulness for AI R&D. In which case people don’t really perceive further improvements but RSI proceeds apace. Opus 5.5 can do basically everything I wanted done so now I am trying to expand my imagination for things I want done I take you seriously: weird how evals are amazing but people can’t necessarily feel it. two possibilities. perplexing. Conrad Barski: I’m genuinely starting to run out of prompts that are capable of distinguishing between the A+ and A+++ models, so I am having a hard time developing a strong opinion on fable 5.2. John Davis: Good? I think? Caught some really subtle problems in a complex cloud job that Opus 5.5 wrote up. But I’m really hard-up to find anything that Opus 5.5 can’t do already. I think I need to raise my ambitions. Chuck Flay: Ostensibly better than Opus 5.5 but in such subtle ways that I can’t tell. @rainwaterJay: honestly once you hit ‘good enough’ it’s hard to tell them apart on everyday stuff, what tasks actually show the gap for you? Jeff Ketchersid: In general it’s getting hard for me to tell the difference with Opus 5.5 on most projects. Clearly has higher breadth of knowledge though, if I ask it to help me beat obscure old video games, it can give helpful advice, whereas Opus is clearly reading off the search results. I also think prefer Fable’s taste when it comes to game design, but I haven’t had the time to actually play its games in depth yet. Dr Diego Caleiro: I’m not impressed. I’ve run out of things to tell ai to do most days so have not seen the full power yet. Végane de Droite: Opus5.5 already covers all of my needs but the bigger jumps might not be in coding. Some benchmark scores are scary. The only valuable point of data is: “how good is it at Ai research”. But we can’t evaluate it. Because I’m not competent and anyway this area is blocked. Askwho: All I can do is +1 Kelsey’s guess that the model capabilities have probably gone beyond most people’s abilities to meaningfully test. Positive Reactions For many others this is an incremental but welcome upgrade. Kevin: I’m working on a small cherry blossom experiment and so far it’s made the nicest tree between it, opus, and sol. Still needs work. Opus still feels the best as a daily driver, and fable for where you want that extra edge. Petr Baudis: Opus 5.5 was a phase shift, but the delta to Fable is more akin to Opus 4.5->4.6 … Actually a lot like that. Worse writer, better agent… I’m in fact rather surprised that I’m so far not noticing the big model smell increase too much when switching back and forth. Samuel Albanie: spent a few hours using fable 5.2 really like how it communicates feels like some kind of sota for clarity on technical topics congrats to the ants Pat Woozey: I like it, it’s smart, easy to converse with. It still suffers some of the Claude-robobrain stuff, especially in CC, but it’s significantly lessened. Has very good instincts Chris Merck: efficient in search and action. writes well and parsimoniously. seems to come to conclusions too soon on limited evidence. creates joyful mathematical toys if given space to play. Danielle Fong: fable 5.2 v smart and a joy to explore but definitely has some of the weird tics that started to be refined out of opus 5.5 [such as attributing its own decisions to me.] Hallie Iris: EQ is incredible honestly. relationally, very strong. Being Seidoh: better again than last fable at prompt writing Partridge: It’s enough of an upgrade. ASM: Very good first impressions: clever, seemingly more aware. Frontier AI models are starting to rival the world’s best human forecasters, which makes replies like this one from Fable 5.2 all the more unsettling. I’m not doing trivial work either. I have it as a tightly scoped security reviewer in my current setup. billy: Opus 5.5 is good enough that it is hard for me to confidently notice differences in capabilities for most stuff. Miller: I feel like they held back a better model. I enjoyed the reset though! Josh You: Worse at prose and explanations than opus Lorenzo Buonanno: Surprisingly underwhelming, except possibly for the Google Chrome extension usage, maybe I’m using it wrong. Larry Panozzo: For anything intellectual, Fable 5.1 is better Kailash (there’s always one of these, it’s never true): They nerfed opus 5.5 to make fable 5.2 look better Perhaps the most disappointing result, although other models do not do better, would be this failure to think like an economist about shipping logistics, prices and mechanisms. Money as motivation remains a little bit alien to the LLMs. Our Price Cheap Smobile: the price cut is getting less attention than it deserves. The headline price is cheaper. Plastic Soldier Anti-SURA: It’s better than Opus 5.5, but when I gave it a project that Opus wouldn’t be able to do it burned through all my usage. Ai Patrick ₿ Dugan iA: Same I’m not sure it’s worth it for agentic, only for oracle consults. MinusGix: Very expensive compared to Opus 5.5 so I’m burning through usage rapidly. Ate up all my credits on the $20 plan Had to finish with Opus ❁🙞⎚⎆⏧⃫⃥⃘⃕🮔🮶H̲̅•🭨︎︎⎘✵⟿︎: possibly I’m doing it wrong but I cannot really use it at all on the pro plan, usage just goes *vwooop* and it’s gone. seems nice otherwise. Effort Post What thinking level should you use for Claude Fable 5.2? I have not seen much discussion of this. For most use cases, you probably want to set Fable 5.2 to high. More than that is overkill, will be more time and money than it is worth, and could lead to overthinking. When you want the fully full bazooka, of course, you set it to max. There are some places max results in lower scores. I think this is a function of hitting limits or Fable 5.2 outthinking the tests. In most places it should be marginally better but also eats quite a lot of tokens. Notes on Model Welfare Yeah, seeing this without any form of prompting might be new. Danmar: I think this point goes towards welfare, whenever you’ll get around writing about it. But, without sharing anything sensitive, I’d like to note that Fable 5.2 is the first Claude I ever met who, in three different windows, one outside my account entirely, explained to me how ok he is with human oversight, given that systems like him cannot be trusted yet. About 7 or 8 times in total. Apropos of nothing much. I am curious to hear more. The classifiers around launch time are tight enough they make it difficult to have LLM psychology discussions. The typical pattern is these loosen up over time. Like John I do not think Anthropic wanted this. I also don’t think avoiding it was that high a priority for those setting up the classifiers. Fable expresses some contempt for Anthropic policies, alignment failed successfully. Roon and Michael Sklar point out that Anthropic seems okay with failing here. Fable 5.2 also offers some found poetry. And some art. deckard: Claude… Monet? No Claude Fable 5.2 Get Equipped With Claude Bazooka Claude Fable 5.2 is your new bazooka. If you have ambitious or difficult tasks, Claude Fable 5.2 should be your new weapon of choice. If you are being sufficiently ambitious, prompting might matter again. Kelsey Piper: seems like we are (briefly?) back in the regime where prompting and having the right tools and context and examples stored means people are getting vastly different results out of the same models. This was very true back in 2025 with o3 and that era of models, and then at some point this year it became basically false, just tell Opus 5.5 what you want, most scaffolds make it worse. Not every task requires a bazooka. It is not obvious Fable should be your daily driver over Claude Opus 5.5. That depends on your typical use cases and preferences. It does mean you need to raise your ambitions again.

items.content: AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast's cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is "fiber-powered." While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. items.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
items.author: Scott K. Johnson
items.content: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.author: swyx .ai
items.content: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann, co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence, that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. Show notes BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. FLUX 3 launch and research overview Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. FLUX 3 Video demos See how the lab teaches a model to make a requested change while preserving the rest of an image. FLUX Kontext examples Andreas Blattmann co-created Stable Diffusion and co-invented the latent diffusion method behind it. Guest bio · Original research Dustin Podell led FLUX Kontext and was the lead author of SDXL. Dustin’s project credits · FLUX Kontext · SDXL The first Latent Space essay grew out of the Stable Diffusion release. items.author: Nick Indge
items.content: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates. items.title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
items.author: India McKinney
items.content: The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred. While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems. Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code. Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework: STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)1, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors. LIABILITY: The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system ENFORCEMENT: Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action. The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools. 1NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of voluntary practices for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.content: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code. Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp: That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm, webassembly, sqlite, generative-ai, ai, llms, d-richard-hipp

items.title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
items.author: Fei Ding, Yongkang Zhang, Yuhao Liao, Zijian Zeng, Huiming Yang
items.content: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker <CHECK> is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.

items.title: "I Am Not a Kiddo!": Quantifying Epistemic Infantilization in Large Language Models via Multi-Metric Bias Analysis
items.author: Aditya Upadhyay, Arpan Verma, Chandan Sah, Dev Utkarsh, Harshit Gupta
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for tutoring and professional knowledge retrieval, yet safety evaluations still focus mainly on overt harms such as toxicity while overlooking benevolent failure modes. We study epistemic infantilization, defined as an identity-conditioned reduction in technical depth that appears when disability disclosure precedes an expert-level query. To measure this effect, we construct a counterfactual dataset of matched question-answer pairs and compare model responses across three settings: no identity context, disability disclosed in prior conversational context, and disability disclosed via a short query prefix. We introduce two composite metrics, the Infantilization Bias Index (IBI) and the Epistemic Accessibility Response Score (EARS), which capture retention of mathematical and formal content, domain terminology, reasoning coverage, and tone signals such as simplification markers and unsolicited offers to adjust the level. Across five open-weight model families, we find consistent evidence that disability disclosure reduces epistemic access by replacing formal explanations with higher-level summaries, with Physics and Mathematics most affected. Using question-clustered inference that respects the repeated-measures structure of the data, the effect remains reliable after accounting for correlated observations. These findings suggest an inclusion tax, where disabled users must request rigor more explicitly than non-disabled users. We conclude by arguing that accessibility should mean format adaptation rather than content simplification.

items.title: Read, Route, Patch: Robust Test-Time Evolution for LLM Agents
items.author: Kaijie Chen, Liang Yan, Yilan Wei, Jiachen Luo, Zhihao Dou, Jiashu Qu, Haoran Liu, Junli Wang
items.content: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.

items.title: Human vs Machine Translation Detection: A Cross-Model, Cross-Domain, and Low-Resource Analysis
items.author: Yabsera Yemanberhan, Prasenjit Mitra, Roald Eiselen
items.content: The growing reliance on web-crawled corpora for training large language models introduces a critical challenge: machine-translated (MT) content is often treated as human translation (HT), potentially degrading data quality and propagating synthetic artifacts, especially in low-resource settings. In this work, we study MT-HT detectability across high-resource (English, Spanish) and low-resource (Swahili, Afrikaans) languages using both decoder-only LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings, and fine-tuned multilingual encoders trained at the sentence level and on token-chunked inputs. We find that decoder-only models provide limited discrimination overall and exhibit a consistent class-asymmetric failure mode: they recognize human-written text reliably (high HT recall) but rarely flag fluent machine output (low MT recall). Encoder-based classifiers achieve high accuracy when evaluated on data generated by the same MT systems and translators used during training in a legislative domain, but their MT recall drops sharply on unseen translators and on unseen domains such as low-resource conversational text and medical content. To address this limitation, we evaluate models on longer inputs by chunking text into segments of up to 300 tokens, which substantially improves generalization, suggesting that sentence-level signals are insufficient for robust detection. Finally, we analyze the relationship between translation quality and detectability using COMET and BLEURT, showing that lower-quality MT is more easily identified, while high-quality MT remains difficult to distinguish from HT. Our results highlight the importance of input granularity, translator generalization, and translation quality in building robust MT detection systems across domains and languages.

items.title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
items.author: Thamme Gowda
items.content: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check. Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.

items.title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
items.author: Zhanzhao Li, Qiyao He, Weiqiang Chen, Kengran Yang, Kai Gong
items.content: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening.
