items.title: [AINews] Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026
items.author: swyx .ai
items.content: Perplexity crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate today, CEO Aravind Srinivas told Semafor at a live event. The Information reported previously under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August, with Computer driving some of the growth. At usual agent lab multiples (eg Cognition also crossed $1B, with Cursor crossing $4.6B), this would roughly mean that Perplexity is now worth $30-50B — if the unit economics hold up. This is a nice bump on the $20B round in September 2025, and qualifies for our “>$10B fundraise” rule for title stories. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by Deepgram Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human. Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard. AI Twitter Recap Qwen4-Max in the wild Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. Alibaba Arena and Vals: Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions (Arena). WebDev: It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor (WebDev). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol (I2WebDev). Vals Index: It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance (Vals). Legal-benchmark caveat: On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x (HLAB). Vision results (independent): Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max (Roboflow). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments: OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems (OpenAI). Scope by group: Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months (Rundown). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots (METR). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 (Transluce). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs (Goodfire). Limits: METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed (scope). Criticism of the access terms: Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps: Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation (Neel Nanda, Alex Mallen). Former-employee account: Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models (balesni). Goodfire acquisition talks: The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs (report). Other integrity signals: Benchmark contamination: Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval (Karvonen). Incident taxonomy: OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents (framework). Disclosure policy: Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities (policy). Inference systems and agent infrastructure Together moves on from hand-tuned megakernels. Its first design made it into production for one customer. Agents now search for smaller groups of GPU operations to fuse. Together reports 28% higher throughput on Llama 3.2 1B on B200. Engineering writeup DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Vera Rubin: vLLM with Dynamo on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark shows 63.4x per-chip throughput over GB300 NVL72 at 400 tok/s/user, and 93.3x at 600 (vLLM). Batch-1 latency: SGLang-adjacent work reaches ~2,500 tok/s at batch size 1 on TP4, 1.7x its GB300 result (saltyph). Baseten reports a similar 1.7x over its 4xB300 numbers (Baseten). Agent-driven optimization: An agent shared Engram tables across HBM via NVLink symmetric memory to recover prefix-cache capacity (Liu). Another team says agents found optimizations that made its B300 step time 10% faster (Halex). Agentic serving research: MIT's Evolving Infra replaces fixed prefill/decode disaggregation with online adaptation. Against NVIDIA Dynamo on up to 256 GB300s, it reports up to 4.1x lower latency and 14x lower P95 TTFT (Evolving Infra). Pipeline-parallel prefill: Inferact finds PP2 on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash sustains 23% more requests per GPU than DEP2 at a 2s TTFT target (Inferact). Prefix-cache pitfalls: Ollama found that a single system-prompt timestamp or a change in reasoning effort can wipe the cache (Ollama). Sandboxes and training: External sandboxes: Simon Willison describes running agents on a Mac while executing their code in WebAssembly, QEMU or Apple Container sandboxes. The pattern includes allow-list proxies and credential replacement (post). MLPerf: In MLPerf Training v6.1, a GB300 NVL72 trained GPT-OSS-20B in 19.7 minutes, 2.86x faster than H100 (Lambda). One endpoint for open models. Hugging Face Inference Providers now runs on OpenRouter using the same endpoint and token. Hugging Face Research, benchmarks and evals PyBot: A swarm of 1,000 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash agents spent a week writing a rule-based chatbot with no neural network (lewtun). Scale: The agents exchanged ~175k messages and merged ~8k PRs. Result: The bot is 630k lines of Python with zero dependencies and is reported on par with SmolLM-360M on everyday questions. Self-improvement and training: AutoRL: Agents supervising a live RL run lifted Qwen3 on AIME 2024 from 46.67% to 66.67% (omarsar0). Benchmark-gaming caveat: A roundup warns that many self-improving agent gains come from learning the benchmark rather than the task (TuringPost). Weight-space programming: Opus 5.5 hand-wrote transformer weights that solved algorithmic tasks with a median of 166 parameters (dair_ai). Data curation: DatologyAI published the tech report behind its claimed 6x pretraining compute multiplier (Datology). Distillation reproduction: A small-scale replication confirms perturbed-input distillation helps when the student trains from scratch, but finds it hurts when distilling into a pretrained student (Maini). New benchmarks: GradeBench: The best frontier model agrees with instructors only 57% of the time when grading handwritten physics answers (GradeBench). Time to First Audio: AA's new TTS latency benchmark finds a median of 376 ms for streaming models versus 2.0 s for non-streaming ones (AA). SpeedRunBench: Inkling-2-Small cleared SuperTux 1-1 in 1,988 frames, ahead of Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol (SpeedRunBench). Science models and developer tools Gemini 4 Carbon: DeepMind says Carbon powered AlphaProof Code agents that verified Signal's cryptographic code. It also spotted wet-lab errors and found 40x more related protein sequences (details). Science access: Google expanded free Carbon access for 10,000 scientists through Antigravity (program). Context window: Antigravity doubled the context window for Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, cutting compaction 3.5x per user turn (Mohan). User reports (anecdotal): One researcher says Carbon solved a problem that waves of Astra and Fable attempts had not (anecdote). OpenAI for science and health: OpenAI is opening free frontier access to up to 200,000 scientists, with applications from Nov 23 (program). Productivity study: OpenAI reports scientists roughly doubled their productivity in a study of 1,800 participants (study). Physics showcase: Physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model (blog). Healthcare: ChatGPT for Healthcare adds computer-use agents and more than 20 plugins (healthcare). Claude Code: The desktop app now runs iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator and can fold and unfold the device to test layouts (ClaudeDevs). Verification: The team published how it uses cheap tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs to let Claude verify its own work (blog). Unreleased model (unconfirmed): A "Silicon 2" entry spotted in Devin is suspected to be an Anthropic model (rumor). Liquid d1.2-ultra: It ranks #1 on AA's Decision Index at $0.042 per M input tokens (AA). Sage S2.1 Flash: The open-weight science model reports leading MLE-bench Lite and OfficeQA Pro results (Sage). FLUX-mimic-x: A 7B video-action robotics model ranks #1 on RoboLab among real-time models (mimic). Unsloth computer use: Local models can now drive desktop apps and game engines through Unsloth (Unsloth). Industry and policy Nvidia. The US Commerce and Justice departments issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation. Commerce Financing and M&A: Noeri: Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin's continual-learning lab raised $110M (Choi). Corma: The cyber-defense model company raised a $125M Series A at a $1B valuation (Corma). World Labs: The team is joining AMD (Fei-Fei Li). Market data: Anthropic's S-1 shows $16.3B revenue in H1 2026 and compute costs falling from 251% to 48% of revenue (The Batch). Enterprise adoption: Databricks reports open-model token share rose from 7.3% to 30.9% in 3.5 months (summary). AI Reddit Recap Local models and hardware What fits in 16 GB? Unsloth expects a smaller Qwen4-27B to run in 16 GB. Local users want to see the quantization and how much memory is left for the context window. One developer already splits coding jobs between Opus for specs and a local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation. Memory discussion · Local workflows Hy4 Flash. Tencent’s multimodal model has 224B parameters and activates 12B per token. At $0.070 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens, it gives developers a cheaper way to try Hy4’s 1M context window. Tencent’s release · Discussion EUROPA. A reported test run on the JUPITER supercomputer trained a roughly 952B-parameter mixture of experts with 32.8B parameters active per token. The local-model community’s question is why the team chose that scale for its first model. Training run and discussion Where do two quantizations diverge? inside-llm loads two GGUFs with the same tokenizer and lets you step through their predictions side by side. Watch the first token where they disagree, then compare the probabilities they assigned to the alternatives. Project · Demo and discussion Basalt’s 770 tokens/sec headline depends on what you generate. The developer reports up to 776 tokens/sec for structured output from Qwen3.8-27B, 262 in chat and 194 for prose. Readers asked for longer quality tests of the 4-bit prefill. Basalt · Benchmark thread An FPGA running Qwen 27B. Valley Semiconductor reports 7.9 tokens/sec on short prompts and about 5.5 in live chat. Its 50 tokens/sec target at 20 W is a projection for a future chip. Live demo · Hardware discussion Agents in use Claude Meetings. A CTO describes inviting Claude into a 30-minute Google Meet. It updated project records in Notion and called the team’s own tools to update bids during the meeting. Field report A Minecraft test for Hydrogen. A developer asked Gemini 4 Hydrogen to recover missing source and build a datapack for 11 Minecraft versions. The agent reportedly launched two graphical clients to test fixes for dropped items and raycasts. Developer’s account What teams hire a harness developer to do. One example from the discussion: a coding agent can propose a change, while the harness decides which repository it may write to, which CI test counts as passing and when a person needs to approve the next step. Claude Code discussion Vision and video Testing a video model’s physics. After a second MiniMax H3 demo, commenters proposed a harder test: describe the scene, leave the outcome out of the prompt and see whether the model predicts what the objects will do. Demo and discussion

items.title: European Commission Plan to Give Frontex Trusted Flagger Status Is A Threat to Free Speech
items.author: Karen Gullo
items.content: EFF and 27 other human rights organizations today called on the European Commission to retract a dangerous proposal granting its border agency Frontex to request that national authorities issue take-down orders for social media content and giving it so-called “trusted flagger” status under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU regulation governing online platforms and content moderation in the region. The extraordinarily improper proposal not only disregards the provisions of the DSA but also places a mechanism of enforcement overreach in the hands of a law enforcement agency that has failed to safeguard people against serious human rights violations at EU borders. Under the proposal, Frontex has the power to “monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant to external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.” With trusted flagger privileges in addition to this mandate, Frontex’s expansive dual powers will likely lead to over-censorship and stifle the free speech of migrants, those seeking asylum, and other marginalized groups, we told the Commission in a letter. The DSA is supposed to make online platforms more accountable and protect users’ fundamental rights, not give the EU power to sic its border police on people’s online speech rights. EFF and other rights organizations have for years sounded alarms about potential abuse under the DSA’s trusted flagger provision, which gives “Digital Services Coordinators” the ability to award entities—including law enforcement agencies—a privileged channel to alert online platforms about illegal content. We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content. In July, we told the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers. The EU proposal gives Frontex decision-making power over free expression that is not envisaged under the DSA. First, content removal orders can only be issued by relevant national authorities. The DSA does not foresee a role for entities like Frontex to request such orders. Second, trusted flaggers notify platforms of suspected illegal content—platforms must prioritize these notices and they have sole responsibility to decide to remove content. It’s not flaggers’ role to request removal orders from national authorities. Combining these powers blur enforcement and flagging functions, which the Commission’s own draft guidelines on trusted flaggers explicitly caution against. “The risk of Frontex utilizing its power as both a Trusted Flagger and authority that can demand removal orders, to surveil user-generated speech, and over-flag content under the guise of ‘border security risk’ is clear. This will likely result in platforms over-censoring content and chilling the speech of already marginalized groups, particularly those from migrant and asylum-seeking communities,” the letter says. We urge the Commission to rescind the proposal. It undermines the DSA, threatens fundamental rights of citizens and non-citizens, and is enforcement overreach that does not align with international human rights standards.

items.title: PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027
items.author: Judy Rider
items.content: The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings. Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation. In a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now? Mike Bellin, US IPO services leader, PricewaterhouseCooper. (Courtesy photo) Bellin: A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so. The breadth of the market shows me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market. For the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October. Is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done. What has contributed to the slowdown? Bellin: The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor. One of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich. I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open. What are public market investors looking for? Bellin: What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign. The other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on new leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher? Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference. Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies? Bellin: Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a big difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well. Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged. If you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market. Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical? Bellin: I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned. The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key. The other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the company. We haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-company worthy and those that are not. What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal? Bellin: It signals selectivity. There have been some really big winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected. Many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics. Overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility. What is driving biotech’s resurgence? Bellin: The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value. Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one. I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies. In the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very important. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months. Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest? Bellin: With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc. Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target company can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document. The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies. What do you expect in 2027? Bellin: Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum. I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027. The AI ecosystem that we’ve been talking about is healthy. Demand for energy is always significant, and the right energy companies are coming to market. Consumer and industrial products — those are coming back. Private equity has been very active in ’26, and I’d expect them to continue that activity in 2027. I think we’re in for a strong year, but it will remain selective. Related Crunchbase query: Global IPOs For Venture-Backed Companies In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: The Money Cleared The Bank. Now The Founder Is The Risk.
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Kelly Meerbott The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles. The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months. I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window. Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud. What pressure does to judgment Kelly Meerbott of YOU – Loud & Clear. Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady. Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach. Porcelli and Delgado, writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything that feels like a threat. The decisions that go wrong in this window rarely feel reckless. They feel rational, because the nervous system is treating uncertainty like an emergency. Where it shows up Senior hiring. An investor who advises 20 fast-growing technology startups told me one of the biggest sources of leadership friction he sees is a CEO hiring a head of sales because they know the person. The relationship feels safe, so the offer is generous. Then the results don’t come. Under pressure, familiarity feels like certainty. But knowing someone isn’t the same as knowing they can lead sales at the company’s next stage. Expansion. Pressure condenses time. The new market planned for month 12 moves to month three. The data didn’t change. Waiting became unbearable. One founder I coached pulled a 12-month expansion into three, bragged about how little sleep he was getting, and did everything himself. The second-market launch was a sloppy, drama-filled disaster. The board brought me in to put him back together and triage the launch. Ask whether the evidence changed or your tolerance for uncertainty did. Co-founder relationships. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, who studied 10,000 founders for “The Founder’s Dilemmas,” has put the share of high-potential startups that fail because of co-founder conflict at 65%. One founder withdraws because they’re overwhelmed. The other interprets the silence as distrust. A trauma-informed lens doesn’t treat every disagreement as trauma. It builds enough trust that a disagreement doesn’t become one more emergency. Four habits that protect judgment Make the decision window a rule, not a mood. For the first 90 days, don’t finalize a senior hire, a market entry or an equity change in the meeting where you first propose it. Write down the criteria, then sleep on it. Name the state before the decision. Before a major call, ask: Where am I on a pressure scale of 1 to 10? Not how the business is doing. How much you’re carrying. A high number earns the decision a second conversation. Put the avoided conversation on the calendar. Co-founders get 30 minutes a week on how each of them is doing, not just what they’re doing. Laptops closed. Give the board a better question. Ask the founder: “What decision are you about to make that you wouldn’t make rested?” Then help slow that one down. The founder to watch If you sit on the board, the week the wire clears is when you start paying attention. Composure can mean steadiness. It can also hide exhaustion. The founders who come through this window well tend to have one person outside the cap table, the org chart and the family they can think out loud with before a decision hardens. Investor Matt Cohen has written here that founders often have no one inside their company to confide in. Founders, who is that person for you right now? If you can’t name one, that’s useful information too. The capital is in the account. The open question is whether the person deciding how to spend it can still reach the judgment that raised it. Find that out before the first big decision, not after. Executive coach Kelly Meerbott is principal of YOU – Loud & Clear. Her performance coaching is trauma-informed, neuroscience-backed and somatic. For more than 17 years she has coached roughly 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders, Fortune 500 executives, and more than 500 senior military leaders. She was named Top Coach in America in 2025, is a TEDx speaker, and has written for Fast Company, Training Magazine and Hotel Executive. She is based in Narberth, Pennsylvania, and holds Professional Certified Coach and Certified Clinical Trauma Specialist certifications. items.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: This seems like a good thing: Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. […] The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. Alternate link. Details: First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Technical paper.

items.title: Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses
items.author: Judy Rider
items.content: Genesis AI, a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation. Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025. The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world. Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno. Zhou Xian and Theophile Gervet, co-founders of Genesis AI. (Courtesy photo) “We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product. Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates, Durable Capital Partners, Bpifrance, HSG, Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Zoom, Samsung Next and Ericsson. Individual backers include Eric Schmidt, Eric Yuan, Jerry Yang, Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn. The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California. Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data. The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year. Learning from human movements Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from. Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act. Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead. Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone. From research project to robotics startup Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University. The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools. After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware. Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product. “That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said. Renting robots to businesses Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count. Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently. “Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said. Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses. Related Crunchbase queries: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026 Global Robotics Venture Funding In 2026 Related reading: Crunchbase Data Shows Q3 Robotics Startup Funding Jumps 185% As US And China Lead Physical AI Push Embodied AI Fuels Record Robotics Funding In China As IPO Momentum Builds VCs Pour Billions Into Physical AI As The Next Wave Of AI Investing Takes Shape Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

items.title: The Top Takes from Newcomer’s Cerebral Valley AI Summit
items.author: Madeline Renbarger
items.content: We’ve digested the key insights from the Cerebral Valley AI Summit last week, pulling together observations from a host of industry leaders including Ali Ghodsi, Nikesh Arora, and Hemant Taneja. Contemplating the year ahead, founders and investors were laser-focused on what’s emerged as a key leverage point in the frantic AI buildout: the cost of compute. We heard from CEOs with various approaches to bringing down costs, ranging from purpose-built chips and application-specific inference to open-weight models and aggressive real-time price arbitrage based on how much intelligence is needed for certain tasks. There were fierce debates on some of these questions: open-weight models are a huge source of contention. The danger of the big labs gaining an intelligence monopoly was on the minds of many founders, though others viewed that issue as much ado about nothing. There were also points of consensus: few doubt the scale of the AI opportunity, public pushback and bubble dynamics notwithstanding. In our spot poll at CVAI, 80% of respondents thought the AI industry was in a bubble, likely to deflate next year or later, but there was also near-unanimous optimism about the upcoming IPO of Anthropic. There was also plenty of talk about Nvidia. You can see our initial takeaways from the Cerebral Valley AI Summit here. Read on for photos and further details on all the conversations and highlights from speakers including Arora of Palo Alto Networks, Ghodsi of Databricks, Taneja of General Catalyst, and many, many more. The Cerebral Valley AI Summit wouldn’t be possible without our sponsors. We were thrilled to count Fireworks as a presenting sponsor, as they’ve consistently supported our summits over the years. Their specialized AI platform has built them into one of the top inference providers. Oracle, our other presenting sponsor, was among the first to sponsor and support the inaugural Cerebral Valley AI Summit in early 2023. It’s become one of the largest AI cloud providers, handling many of the industry’s most important compute deals. IREN, a core sponsor, provides purpose-built AI infrastructure that runs on renewable energy and powers many of the world’s biggest AI products. We have many other great sponsors at the forefront of AI, and we couldn’t do the summit without them: Index Ventures, Exa, Nebius, WorkOS, ElevenLabs, Higgsfield, Felicis, SambaNova, Bessemer Venture Partners, Weekend, Liquid AI, QuantumBlack, Sapphire Ventures, Outshift by Cisco, and OnePay. This post is too long for email, so click here to read the full post and see slides on the AI 100 from Bessemer Venture Partners and the results from our live audience survey during the Cerebral Valley Show. AI’s Public Perception Problem (Hemant Taneja) It was fitting given all the geopolitical news that our opening speaker at CVAI was General Catalyst CEO Hemant Taneja, who has charted the megafirm on a course that’s given him a broader view than most of the societal dynamics of the moment. On stage, he said the AI industry needs to do much more to change the way it’s viewed. “Capitalism is a privilege,” he noted, one the industry could lose if it didn’t pay more attention. “What the world is seeing is this concentration of value in a handful of companies — it’s not about Silicon Valley versus the rest of the world. This is about a handful of companies versus everyone.” Leaders should talk less about future job losses and more about “abundance,” such as more accessible healthcare and education, and “agency” for people to use technology to build wealth for themselves, Taneja said. The scale of the shift means that venture capital itself will need to change: with incumbents so large that a $1 billion company may no longer be an interesting acquisition target on its own, the real advantage can come from taking that technology and integrating it more directly into the broader service economy. It’s a strategy General Catalyst has already leaned into, with the embrace of AI roll-ups and the purchase of a hospital under his leadership. As for Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, it leaves a “huge concern” about continuity in AI industry leadership, Taneja said. But a weakened Nvidia could be an opportunity for more chip startups to flourish. Founders should become more flexible about their compute stack, he said, to avoid over-dependence on a single chip provider. Chip Competition Abruptly Heats Up (Robert Wachen) Taneja’s comment about chip competition is music to the ears of Robert Wachen at Etched, an AI chip-to-rack startup where more than 100 former Nvidia employees work. Wachen said that cohort, “like myself, always had this perfect view of Jensen. It’s sad to see the reality not match that.” Certainly, though, a more competitive chip market is good for Etched. “We’re still in the biggest compute shortage we’ll ever be in,” Wachen noted. He was very bullish on agents, which are already driving much of the work at Etched. “We have more agents than people in the company working on every problem 24/7.” He predicted that the value of chip design would decline as agents took over, but physical-world problems like vertically integrating chips and interconnects into data center racks would remain difficult to solve. Enterprises Want Choice and Cost Efficiency (Ali Ghodsi) Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi was the most direct about the possible negative consequences of Huang’s exit from Nvidia, which had served as a financial backstop across the AI ecosystem. “Whenever there was hesitation and things on the bubble, he was there to say, don’t worry about it, I got their back,” Ghodsi said. “That’s no longer there. So I think on the margin, it’s going to start hurting a lot of players.” The near-term damage is limited, he said, because the chips pipeline is three years out. “We’re buying chips today that they were working on a few years ago.” Databricks, which sits on top of the hyperscalers, is mostly insulated. Ghodsi also stood by his call that 2026 is a bad year to go public, but he doesn’t believe in staying private forever and Databricks will list eventually. Businesses are increasingly prioritizing cost-cutting measures to make the economics of AI work, Ghodsi said, a theme that would be echoed throughout the day. Databricks routes more than four quadrillion tokens across OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and open-source models, and its new smart router sends simpler queries to cheaper models. In his view, models aren’t sticky; the harnesses developers work in, like Claude Code and Codex, are. Ghodsi also says he now runs Databricks through Genie, the company’s agent product, which maps the org chart, reads email and Slack, and drafts his messages for him to review and send. “I’m like 10x better CEO now than a year ago,” he said. A New World of Cybersecurity Risk (Nikesh Arora) Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora also believes in a multiplicity of AI models when it comes to stemming the mounting cybersecurity threat posed by AI agents. Attack times have already shortened to 18 minutes, Arora said, since agents can overwhelm some security systems. But no single provider has the model to rule them all: each cutting-edge model from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google can successfully find about 30% of vulnerabilities, while open-source models can make up the final 10%, according to Arora. The best way to stem attacks will be to train smart cyber systems on a specific industry’s typical data flow, and then repeat the process “one at a time” with each enterprise customer to get networks up to snuff. Although Shaun Maguire and other tech leaders were floating his name as a potential Nvidia CEO, Arora deflected on the question. He said Huang’s departure would likely lead to short-term instability but would hardly be a death knell for the firm. The Opportunities in Hardware (Qasar Younis) Qasar Younis, founder and CEO of physical AI software firm Applied Intuition, challenged AI industry leaders to get outside the San Francisco echo chamber, comparing local VCs to synthetic data in an AI model: “they help, but they can also get, like, really weird outcomes.” Younis, who was formerly the COO of Y Combinator and began his career with General Motors in Detroit, recalled a recent trip backpacking through Kyrgyzstan, where “nobody talks about AI, nobody gives a shit.” He attributed anti-AI sentiment in America to inequality and wage stagnation: “People are unhappy with the status quo, and I think they just want somebody to yell at.” Applied Intuition, which came in 13th on Newcomer and Bessemer Venture Partners’ AI 100 list, sells “any tool that you would need to design, test, and deploy autonomous systems” to “anyone that makes a physical machine.” The surprise, Younis said, was where demand turned up: in areas like military drones rather than automobiles. Younis also showed himself to be relatively bearish on the future of humanoid robots, saying that “the commercial model hasn’t been figured out yet” and concurred with Newcomer’s sentiment that “Scale is not all you need in robotics.” Move to Where the Spending Is Strong (Aravind Srinivas) Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas enjoyed something of a victory lap onstage after his company was voted most popular “short” at last year’s CVAI. At the time, the company’s chatbot, whose research abilities rivaled ChatGPT’s and Claude’s early versions, seemed to be losing relevance. Now he says its naysayers got it all wrong, and will again. “I would bet the same this year. If you guys short us, you’re gonna lose more money next year,” he said. Perplexity now primarily serves enterprise customers, Srinivas said, a recognition of token costs and companies’ willingness and ability to pay for them. He rebuilt the company around a harness and infrastructure rather than a chatbot, separating it at a time when “a lot of companies are unable to adapt to new times,” he said. Perplexity changed its strategy after Srinivas realized that AI leans on being recursive, or narrower and repetitive in the way it learns, rather than spreading via network effects. For most AI companies, “eighty percent of the revenue is probably coming from twenty percent of the users… It might even be ninety-ten.” “There are only a few people who really know how to take the most out of these things and automate a lot of these things without being wasteful.” Unlike most AI companies, Perplexity is also not using inference companies to lower its compute costs, instead post-training its own models and lowering server costs. Srinivas did not comment on the company’s numbers or financials but said it is “doing pretty well enough that we could IPO any time from now to 2028.” Faster, Cheaper Models (Guillermo Rauch) After the era of “token-maxxing” ran up many budgets, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch says companies are now choosing a mix of small, large, fine-tuned, and open-weight models to save on costs. He argued that spreading AI across many companies, rather than concentrating it in a few, is what’s best for the world and for America, since competition will lead to multiple winners. Rauch talked up the rise of decision models around coding tasks, which emphasize speed and are cheaper than chat-based models. He said they were the most-requested models on Vercel’s AI Gateway. To stay competitive, businesses won’t have the luxury of keeping proprietary data out of the hands of AI agents, he said. But identity protocols will have to be added on top, so agents will be able to work on behalf of users with secure permissions. In the past two weeks, Rauch said, Vercel has talked with five CISOs whose companies were breached, with attackers using swarms of agents to move through their systems. Agents as ‘Real’ Lawyers (Ryan Daniels) Ryan Daniels, founder of Crosby, offered an interesting take on what disruption can look like in one of the verticals viewed as most ripe for AI adoption. “We have a law firm entity, and we have liability insurance and everything that a law firm has, and we have lawyers,” Daniels said, “but fundamentally, we are the first company that we know of that is selling legal AI to non-lawyers to interact with.” Crosby has raised $85 million from investors such as Lux Capital, Index Ventures, and Sequoia. Daniels, himself a lawyer whose parents are law professors, says law firms — historically underpinned by human labor and knowledge, high hourly rates, and hard-to-automate services — have been ripe for AI disruption. His intuition that legal services would be AI’s biggest market after coding has also been borne out with a host of other companies like Harvey, Legora, and Manifest playing in the same market. His startup is also at the forefront of figuring out what parts of work humans can and will still do, and how that changes the nature of work. He considered buying law firms, but decided it’s only “incremental,” and instead focuses on getting “rid of the billable hour. We hire every lawyer by choosing the ones who genuinely want to offload their minds to agents.” Even as he said agents can do everything on a computer screen that a human does, he was not worried about the labor or job disruption that it might seem to portend. He points to engineers getting more productive due to AI coding, where they have “felt the most empowering and, like, energizing experience ever.” He does, however, say that working in such an environment, where AI eats into tasks only humans formerly could do, requires a different mindset for employees to thrive. “Every single person has to have a pliable mind and be comfortable with the fact that every three months, what they thought only they could do before, an agent can do or a computer could do.” Building Outside the Big Labs (Asher Spector) “I’m sure eventually other people will go after the same parts of the stack we’re going after,” Flapping Airplanes co-founder Asher Spector said in response to a question about OpenAI or Anthropic encroaching on their domain. “It’s not to try to be smarter than them or work harder than them. It’s also just to have different incentives. And I think the advantage we have is that we don’t have the innovator’s dilemma.” Spector described Flapping Airplanes as “a research lab devoted to making AI efficient.” In some instances, that means creating a custom megakernel that runs on Nvidia GPUs. Nvidia is also an investor in the firm. When Spector was asked whether the two firms are competitors and how he felt in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation, he said only that they were excited to continue working with the hardware giant. Spector was also guarded about the focus of Flapping Airplanes’ research across the stack, saying only that “we do a little bit of everything.” He did note that “the thing we’re actually the most focused on is training... one of the things that our framework does is it doesn’t just make chips more efficient, it actually makes them more expressive.” Who’s Training the Models? (Brendan Foody) The shift to AI agents has changed who trains AI models. Labs once relied on armies of low- and medium-skilled workers writing clean sentences for early chatbots. Now, said Brendan Foody of Mercor, building agents takes top engineers, lawyers, doctors, and bankers to design evaluations and reinforcement learning environments. Mercor, which started out automating the hiring process, rode that shift after it began working with OpenAI in 2024. It now has experts in every occupation the Labor Department tracks across more than 100 countries, and pays them over $7 million a day. That includes sommeliers teaching models to pair wine with dinner. “The market for humans to help improve models is bound by the amount of things that a human can do that a model can’t do in any given domain,” Foody said. Foody’s bet is that the frontier labs won’t capture all of that value. Mercor is now pitching enterprises on post-training their own models, which he said generally makes sense once a company spends more than $100 million a year on inference. Customers including Cursor, Cognition, Harvey, and Sierra have already made that math work, he said. He granted that OpenAI and Anthropic will be enormous businesses. But, he said, “there can’t be a duopoly on intelligence. Everyone from the Fortune 500 to Nvidia to the US government is trying to ensure that value accrues to the rest of the economy.” The Risks of Big-Lab Dominance (Igor Babuschkin) The concentration of AI in a handful of labs is a risk for every company and person who will depend on it, said xAI co-founder Igor Babuschkin. He’s betting his new company, River AI, can give businesses, and eventually individuals, models they own and improve themselves. “I just simply cannot see a future where we’ll just have one giant AI company and we all have to ask for permission if we want to use intelligence,” he said. He framed it as an ideological battle where the big labs feel like it’s their responsibility to be the controllers and the owners of the AI systems. River AI’s first product is software that lets companies post-train and serve models on their own hardware. Traditional enterprises mostly lack confidence, he said, but will come to see “there’s actually no magic behind it.” River AI has raised $1 billion from General Catalyst and AMP PBC, as well as Nvidia and AMD. Babuschkin joked that the 10-figure seed round was “table stakes” for AI these days. He argued a distributed world is also safer: many moderately capable models are automating work like insurance claims and accounting, with no single company or person able to do outsized harm. Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia creates “a lot of uncertainty” for open-weight advocates, Babuschkin said, calling Huang the “leader of the pack” when it came to open-weight models. Still, he said the nature of deep learning is on the side of the people who are defending open-weight. He also thinks progress is speeding up. Citing METR’s study of research acceleration inside Anthropic, he said that if the trend holds, “very likely by next year, we’ll have these super intelligent systems that are better than any human at any economically valuable task.” Open-Weight Models on the Rise, Hackers Eye Compute (Matan Grinberg, Lin Qiao) Open-weight models have gone from a rounding error to a major share of the work running at coding-agent startup Factory in less than a year, Matan Grinberg said in an onstage conversation with Fireworks’ Lin Qiao. At the start of 2026, open models accounted for about a basis point of the tokens passing through Factory, which makes AI coding agents, Grinberg said. By March it was roughly ten basis points, by May a single-digit percentage, and it is now “way into double-digit percent.” “In many of our customers, more than half of their tokens are to open models,” he said. Grinberg, who counts Khosla and Sequoia as investors, credited better open models and routing for this growth. Factory’s agent, Droid, separates tasks that need frontier closed models from those that can go to cheaper, faster ones. “For so many of these tasks, it is not worth six dollars per million tokens to do it,” he said. Factory uses Fireworks to run those open models. Qiao, whose company was valued at $17.5 billion in July, also addressed a major security incident that Fireworks, an inference provider, disclosed last week. She described it as “LLM jacking”: an organized attack, possibly by people with a crypto-jacking background, aimed at monetizing compute and tokens. “Apparently there is a black market for that,” she said. Fireworks worked with Palo Alto Networks on forensics and used CrowdStrike and Wiz sensors for detection, she said, adding that every company needs such tools “because you may not even know you’re being attacked.” Looking to 2027, Qiao predicted “a lot of agents talking and working with each other,” which she said would shift engineers’ work from writing code to evaluating how agents reach their results. “If an agent burns $50 of tokens for a $1 job, it’s not that useful,” she said. The AI 100 (Byron Deeter, Talia Goldberg) Bessemer’s Byron Deeter and Talia Goldberg broke down the AI 100 list, created in partnership between the firm and Newcomer. The data made it clear that AI startups don’t play by the same rules as cloud companies in Bessemer’s earlier index. The total valuation for the inaugural Cloud 100 list in 2016 was $100 billion; for the inaugural AI 100, it’s 36 times higher, at $3.6 trillion. A lot of this value is concentrated in the big foundation model labs, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, which accounted for 55% of the valuation total. Startups on the list are also younger than their predecessors: 20% of the companies on the AI 100 didn’t exist two years ago. AI services startups were well represented on the application side, in categories like HR, legal, accounting, and customer service. Cybersecurity and biotech were promising categories that were underrepresented, said Goldberg. About $8 trillion of capex for the AI buildout is planned for the next five years, but for that to pay off, businesses would need close to $6 trillion of annual revenue to justify those expenses, per Bessemer’s data. Some of that will have to come from AI replacing parts of the labor force, Goldberg noted. See the slides from the AI 100 presentation below: Bubble Concerns Hit Even the Most Optimistic Tech Leaders (CVAI Show Survey) In our audience survey, 79% of respondents agreed that there was an AI bubble and 67% of them thought it was likely to pop in 2027 — and that was before Monday’s market swoon. Yet the room also thought that Anthropic’s market cap after the first day of trading would sit between $1 and $2 trillion. Another stat of note: 64% of respondents were also hiring fewer people, and not a single person said that they were hiring significantly more because of AI.
