items.title: Jensen Huang Really Liked Selling China Advanced AI Chips
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: This scandal is a really big deal. Jensen Huang has resigned after multiple affairs came to light, one of them with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang who also helped smuggle billions in Nvidia chips, and another with a direct report at Nvidia. The most important scandal around Jensen Huang has been known for a long time to those paying attention. Jensen Huang and Nvidia have for years treated America and the United States Government as adversaries. They have engaged in a long running and brutal lobbying and influence campaign, both privately and publicly, to capture relevant government policy to allow Nvidia to sell as many as possible of its most advanced chips to China, and to allow China to otherwise use those chips via a combination of chip smuggling and remote access. They have compromised the integrity of our government, potentially quite broadly, as well as the national security of the United States of America. They have greatly hurt our relative position in the ‘AI race.’ In addition to the considerations of national security and our strategic interest, this has forced our AI companies to push forward faster and harder, and made sane AI policy much harder. When Jensen Huang chose to have a long-running affair with Alice Huang, he knew that she was central to the diversion of billions of dollars in high end AI chips to China. His company was active in covering up those actions and in clamping down on official investigations and enforcement. He did not need to suspect or know she was a spy to know the nature of his actions regarding her, or his other actions and rhetoric and those of Nvidia in general, and how they directly hurt the national security of the United States. The nice term we used to use for this, back when anyone seemed to care, was corruption. There is also the less nice term that we used to use for such things. Even on Monday we learned of yet another covert influence operation by Nvidia to promote them selling chips to China in order to ‘ensure US, not Chinese-made chips, continue to dominate the AI market.’ After several days in which Alice Huang’s status as a Chinese spy was not in dispute, we now have pushback from various sources that Alice Huang may not have formally been a Chinese spy. The ODNI people near Clayton called that description ‘not quite accurate.’ The CIA sources say the intercepts do not ‘show her knowingly pass information to China.’ Himes expressed doubt. It is possible that she was not formally recruited, and did not share intel with the CCP. If true, this hopefully would mean there was not additional loss of intelligence or other things due to this relationship. I would put my current p(spy) at clearly over 50%, but less than 95%, and do not see much value in trying to refine further. Trump is now saying he doesn’t know she’s a Chinese spy, after many days of (like everyone else) conspicuously not saying that. In my experience, if we did not have good reason to presume she was a spy, it would not have taken this long for people to start denying it. Other than Himes, those denying the reports have a direct interest in casting doubt on her status as a spy, including to explain their own inaction. Himes said ‘lawmakers still lack enough to tell’ how Alice acted, but that is entirely consistent with simply not having been sufficiently briefed. So okay, now the arrow says ‘suspected of’ spying, out of an abundance of caution. Does putting ‘suspected of’ there change the overall picture? Is that the only thing you should put in that arrow, as opposed to for example ‘smuggled chips for’? (Also, this is missing the third ‘alleged’ affair. There’s always more stuff.) Or this graph, originally from Bloomberg? Even if it turns out she was not part of the formal Chinese spy network, she was acting as a de facto Chinese agent. Her primary mode of doing business was still the smuggling of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s top AI chips, and allowing China to access them. It also does not change what Jensen Huang should have believed or done from his epistemic position. Nor does it change that he had three affairs that we know about, one of which was with a major customer illegally smuggling billions in chips and the other two with Nvidia employees including at least one direct report. If you wish, you can retroactively qualify or modify all my related statements about Alice Huang accordingly. Given her role in chip smuggling and sales, I do not believe this materially changes my conclusions about Nvidia or Jensen Huang. Table of Contents The Story That Matters Most. Yes Export Controls Matter and Are Finally Happening. How Far Does This Go? The First Step Is Admitting You Have a Problem. Somehow People Are Still Defending Jensen Huang. Jensen Huang Wants to Call It a Comeback. On Interim CEO Kress. An Actual Attack on Jensen’s Character. Solve for the New Equilibrium. But This Time They’ve Gone Too Far. The Story That Matters Most Miles Brundage is correct to draw the parallel to the situation with Jacob Coxon. Where everyone paying attention has known the basics for a while but we needed a precipitating event to make Nvidia’s and Jensen Huang’s bad faith actions common knowledge. Dmitri Alperovitch: Whether or not Alice Huang had been recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security has always been a tertiary issue. What’s quite clear is that: She has been a large Nvidia customer (and a sexual relationship with her is highly problematic from a corporate policy and governance perspective for Jensen on those grounds alone) She is controlling a shell company Megaspeed dedicated to smuggling compute to both US Govenment-listed Chinese AI companies and to data center build outs in China itself – all in serious violation of US law, potentially making Jensen part of a criminal conspiracy to evade US export controls. She is connected to an entire web of Chinese shell companies trying to do the same. Jensen wasn’t fired because he had an affair with an alleged MSS agent. He was fired because he: Had at least one and now, quite plausibly, multiple affairs with people in his reporting chain in violation of company policy. Something that has gotten numerous CEOs fired over the years, including at Intel and McDonalds. Lied to his board about his relationship and forced the company to put out false statements to the public, putting it in legal jeopardy. Was involved in a sexual relationship with a Chinese smuggler that had violated US export controls laws and provided her with billions of dollars of Nvidia chips that facilitate that criminal activity. By lying and hiding that relationship from his family, the company, and the public, he put himself in a position to be blackmailed by Chinese intelligence services. He very likely ordered his general counsel to interfere in an investigation by US government into his mistress’ smuggling operation. He presided over stunning and extensive compliance failures to investigate and prevent his chips from being smuggled illegally into Chinese mainland and being provided to PLA affiliated institutions, all in violation of US law This is a shocking indictment of him and his record and the board clearly had no alternative but to fire him. Jessica Tillipman: And this is why Nvidia will be one of my leading case studies in my anti-corruption and compliance class this spring. Few case studies include so many issues at the same time: conflicts of interest, third party due diligence, corporate compliance policies, tone at the top, corporate governance, board fiduciary duties, risk management, corporate disclosure obligations, internal investigations, and a growing number of government ethics and accountability issues that we learn more about every day. Jeff Baker Films: What is your take on Jensen resigning because otherwise he would have to sign SOX filings for the earnings report next week and that would have left him criminally liable? Jessica Tillipman: Given what has been reported/alleged, he may already have substantial personal exposure that doesn’t depend on the next filing. So no, I don’t think avoiding the next SOX certification is the primary driver of his resignation. The reason I keep Mike Solana on as a source, despite all his rhetoric, is that underneath it all he calls it like he sees it, so we get statements like this one: Mike Solana: funny that people are blaming jensen’s fall on both anti-asian bigotry, in the reflexively woke corner of the internet, and on something more akin to ‘me too’ overreaching on the based right. anyway, fwiw I think it mostly has to do with the fact that he was fucking a ccp asset. probably it wouldn’t matter if the CEO of olive garden accidentally fucked a spy. mistakes happen. boys will be boys! but we are in an AGI arms race with china, are we not? and they are trying to thwart export controls, are they not? and jensen is a key figure here, is he not? ftr if jensen really did just have a few consensual affairs, the megaspeed / ccp stuff is fabricated, or jensen really didn’t suspect anything, and we discover a reasonable motive for the CIA to destroy him, i’m on board with the persecution narrative. just don’t see that yet. Yes Export Controls Matter and Are Finally Happening Something about a goose chasing you asking why the stocks went down. Noah Smith: Export controls work, and all the people who say “export controls will just make a Chinese tech stronger” are either fools or liars Financial Times: China warns US not to use Nvidia scandal as pretext for tech curbs Shares in Chinese tech giants that have relied on Nvidia chips for developing their AI models fell on Thursday, with Alibaba down 6.8 per cent. Two Chinese large language model providers listed in Hong Kong, Z.ai and MiniMax, sank more than 9 per cent and nearly 8 per cent respectively. Kyle Chan: The market believes Chinese AI companies are still highly dependent on Nvidia chips. Joe Weisenthal: I hadn’t thought to look at the publicly traded Chinese AI companies. But the maker of GLM 5.3 is down by nearly 33% in the last 4 trading days. Oof, the stock is down nearly 89% from its peak this summer. Jensen Huang no longer being CEO of Nvidia is crashing the value of Z.ai. Why? You know exactly why. We kept not getting new export controls because Howard Lutnick kept not allowing them to go forward, forcing Scott Bessent and the NSC to finally go around him in order to issue a remote access rule and to expand restrictions on Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil. Amrith Ramkumar (WSJ): “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said in a release. Rush Doshi: The Trump administration just dropped new remote access rules, no doubt spurred by the Nvidia scandal. In the first paragraph, they made Commerce publish a line effectively indicating the Administration’s lack of faith in Commerce. Remarkable. This way of getting the rule finalized was an unprecedented move, forced by unprecedented refusal to follow either the national interest or the wishes of the President. Amrith Ramkumar (WSJ): “It is unprecedented for a Commerce Department rule to be written by the National Security Council and the Treasury Department,” said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously worked on tech and security issues at the State Department. “The fact that the Commerce Department press release says this shows that Commerce resisted publishing this rule to the bitter end, and was forced to do so by the White House.” We badly need these rules. Nvidia did not even cut off specifically Megaspeed, after they were caught and supposedly put on a ‘no sell’ list, to the extent that this was not even hidden from trade records: Ana Swanson: Both Nvidia and the Commerce Department have now said that Nvidia placed Megaspeed on a “no sell” list in June 2025. But trade data the Times obtained from @importgenius show that, between July 2025 and February 2026, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary received more than $800 million of shipments containing controlled Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s board may at least be pretending to do something about this, now. They have announced a new Oversights Committee. That’ll fix it. Nvidia Newsroom: NVIDIA Board of Directors Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee News Summary Committee to provide oversight over NVIDIA’s national security and global trade compliance programs Committee will retain independent, outside experts to provide legal, national security and trade compliance expertise to support the Committee Director Suzanne Nora Johnson appointed Committee Chair NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. NVIDIA’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the Committee and to Interim CEO, Colette Kress, on day-to-day operations. The Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will also include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. It will meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session. The Committee will oversee the Company’s ongoing efforts to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance. “NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world’s leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” said Harvey Jones, Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors. The decision to create this new committee reflects the Board’s further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight. How Far Does This Go? As Nate Silver says, this story is a really big deal. He argues that the political world, partly due to this being a busy news cycle, is still underreacting to this story. This includes the risk of a major anti-AI backlash. Potentially this goes all the way to the top. Congress will be investigating. There is a strong case that this is the most serious scandal of the Trump era, full stop. Oliver Wiseman: “We spoke with three former Commerce officials who described being sidelined or pushed out of the department during Trump’s term after devising technology restrictions aimed at protecting U.S. national security. One said there was a perception in the department that Nvidia had a hand in at least some of the purges.” Must read on the Nvidia scandal from Matt Pottinger and Liza Tobin. It almost certainly goes as far as Howard Lutnick. Hopefully Lutnick gets removed. Ana Swanson, Tripp Mickle, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan (NYTimes): There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department. … Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels. Mr. Lutnick frequently calls and messages with Mr. Huang, and the department prepares carefully for their private meetings together in Mr. Lutnick’s fifth floor office. All Nvidia matters are routed through Jeff Kessler, a top deputy to Mr. Lutnick, who is said to rarely take any significant action without the commerce secretary’s approval. Nvidia’s general counsel has also been given direct access to shape new rules, including leaving comments in draft regulations affecting the company. … Mr. Lutnick has repeatedly delayed or deferred technology controls, slowing down efforts throughout the year, according to people who described the discussions. Straight up corruption is a plausible hypothesis. … There are also concerns about possible conflicts of interest given that the investment firm that Mr. Lutnick steered for decades, Cantor Fitzgerald, operates in a wide range of industries, from cryptocurrency to data centers, that rely on Nvidia chips and could be affected by rules Mr. Lutnick is currently weighing. That business is now run by Mr. Lutnick’s sons. … The activities of Mr. Lutnick’s sons have been a source of irritation for Mr. Trump and concern for some other Trump advisers, despite the fact that Mr. Trump’s own sons’ businesses have prompted similar criticisms. Alec Stapp: Key points from @ChrisRMcGuire: 1. “It was Mr. Lutnick who made the decision not to enforce export controls designed to counter chip smuggling, making Mr. Huang a potential target.” 2. “It is largely Mr. Lutnick’s fault that Megaspeed, the company that employed the alleged spy, successfully smuggled a reported $7 billion of Nvidia chips into China (a number that no doubt represents the tip of the iceberg).” 3. “Chip smuggling is running rampant. Taiwanese customs data shows that from 2025 to 2026, over $60 billion worth of A.I. chips were most likely shipped to Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, making these 3 relatively small countries among the largest importers of A.I. chips in the world.” 4. “Mr. Lutnick has not added a single company to the entity list, the Commerce Department’s trade blacklist, in over a year, which is the longest stretch without an update in 18 years.” 5. “Mr. Lutnick was reportedly briefed on Mr. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a Megaspeed executive, and her suspected ties with Chinese intelligence services, in May 2026.” 6. “Mr. Lutnick appears to be holding fast on keeping Megaspeed off the blacklist, despite repeated urgings from other members of the administration — including Mr. Trump himself.” 7. “Even worse, senior officials under Mr. Lutnick may have impeded law enforcement investigations into Megaspeed. In May 2025, Jeff Kessler, a top deputy to Mr. Lutnick who oversees export controls, reportedly discussed the department’s ongoing investigation into Megaspeed with Nvidia’s general counsel — a highly unusual action. The department halted its investigation soon afterward.” Potentially it could reach David Sacks, who was the AI Czar and in that position was very clearly de facto functioning as Nvidia’s chief lobbyist and advocate. Kareem Rifai: I think there should be a lot more questions being asked about David Sacks, who spent years furiously lobbying for the US to induce Ukraine’s surrender and then used his position in government to lobby on behalf of giving the CCP unfettered access to Nvidia chips. The First Step Is Admitting You Have a Problem I find this part of the story very much to Huang’s credit. Wall St Engine: Jensen Huang in his last hours as Nvidia CEO, per Bloomberg: > The board met late into the night & left him no choice but to resign > > He looked broken, his take-charge style gone > Started saying things like “whatever” & “I don’t care” > He has since called himself a “piece of sh–” > He says he no longer cares what happens to him > His main concern: his wife, and not “ruining the lives” of the women now linked to him Drake Bennett and Ian King (Bloomberg): A turning point came last Friday, Nov. 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterward, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang’s house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn’t want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. … On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, leaving him with no formal role at the company he co-founded. Alas, he loses most of that credit the minute he starts planning a potential comeback. Somehow People Are Still Defending Jensen Huang There is a logic that goes something like this, and it generalizes beyond Huang: Jensen Huang did these no good, quite bad things, sure. But they never would have come to light like this, and he would have gotten away with it, except for those meddling kids, who told the truth about it. Thus this is character assassination, a government plot, tyranny, must not stand. This comes from a cultural position that of course anyone powerful will have done many horrible things, and of course we do not hold them accountable, so trying to hold them accountable by saying the things they have done must be some evil plot. I disagree. There are also arguments that take this form: Jensen Huang was the founder and CEO. Therefore, Nvidia is his, and if you take it away from him, you need proof that he did something sufficiently horrible, and it’s like a court of law. If it turns out you overcharged him then double jeopardy attaches and he goes free on the lesser included offenses. Which in this case are actually far worse but never mind that. But you can’t formally prove the exact thing in question, so he walks, which means you have to let him continue to run Nvidia. This is an outrage. I mean, come on, OpenAI’s board couldn’t fire Sam Altman, and also I would really like if my board couldn’t fire me. So let’s bring Jensen Huang back. No, seriously. As in: Garry Tan: Jensen deserves due process, not whatever is happening right now. Cate Hall: “what about DUE PROCESS??” is a really funny response to the duly authorized board of a private company making the core decision it exists to make. Again, I disagree. This is madness. The central purpose of the board of directors is to, if necessary, fire the CEO. You also have this great illustration of a deeply twisted worldview twice over: Palmer Luckey (CEO Anduril): China wants Jensen out, so I want him in. China does not want Jensen Huang out, or at least I would be extremely surprised and confused to learn that China wanted that. Jensen Huang has at minimum been quite the ‘useful idiot’ selling them billions in chips, with this scandal and his departure triggering renewed strong calls for export controls on chips. See the section ‘Yes Export Controls Matter’ which is one of a highly continuing series. Why would China want him out? Then there’s the second level. Why do you think it is a good argument, or virtuous, or that it speaks well of you, to publicly say that you want Jensen in because China wants him out? That you think this is a strong argument, without looking at the reasons? That you should want whatever the other guy does not want, because the other guy is a bad man? Which in turn makes you make up stuff about what the other guy wants. I like to think Palmer Luckey does not actually think like that, and instead only thinks that it is beneficial to his social position to present himself as thinking like this, and thus is lying. If he genuinely does think that way, this is far worse. Teortaxes tries to maintain that what ‘has been done’ to Jensen is ‘significantly worse than what happened to Jack Ma.’ Nothing ‘was done’ to Jensen other than to reveal things he most definitely did, and to fire him for those actions. Jensen Huang remains a free man with many billions of dollars. At most, there were overconfident statements about the status of Alice Huang. The rest is clearly true, and the Nvidia board are the ones who removed Jensen Huang. His position was clearly untenable, and would have been untenable either way. I thought all of that was as crazy as it would get. Boy was I wrong. I happened to see this post by Ben Thompson, ‘Obituaries,’ in which he calls this the death of, and I swear I am not making this up: Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, okay, I guess. Nvidia, most valuable company in the world, not technically accurate, but ok. The AI bubble, ‘2025-2027’, ?!, sigh. AI as normal technology and the US Semiconductor industry, 1947-2047, ???. Tech company independence, 1968-2026, no, seriously. American exceptionalism, 1776-2026, no, seriously. What does one even say to something like that, when what happened was ‘tech CEO who treated America as an adversary and facilitated the smuggling of billions in chips while sleeping with the executive in question who is probably also a spy and also a direct report gets summarily and appropriately forced to resign and replaced by the CFO while a search begins, and the Treasury Secretary asks for a new CEO from outside in light of all the rampant crime facilitation and national security issues.’ If this is the end of American exceptionalism or tech company independence, what about [unfurls comically long scroll of events from the second Trump administration, the Biden administration, the first Trump administration, the Obama administration…] Max Read is on point on why some people cannot let this one go, no matter how obviously Jensen Huang is now unfit to be CEO of Nvidia, and how badly this compromised national security. Max Reed: Two ongoing debates in particular, one central to the White House and the other to the AI sector, have been already shaping this story for over a year now: China hawks vs. (expedient) China doves. Open weight vs. closed weight models. Founder class vs. managerial class. To those in the vibe army of the Silicon Valley founder class, they are visionaries who will save the world. Any limits whatsoever on their power, any attempt to impose any form of control on them, is tyranny. Unless you are talking about Dario Amodei, who is himself considered tyranny. All other founder CEOs are to be as Gods. The China dove part is obvious. The weird part about it is that the main reason to be a China dove is so that Nvidia can sell more chips and thus make more money. You know, for the ‘American tech stack.’ That whole China dove position is an Nvidia op first, and only secondarily a China op. Two astronauts. This is then piled on top of the open weight support. Jensen Huang supports open weights, not out of ideology but because he wants to commoditize his complement and does not understand the nature of the risks involved. So these people love him, thinking this is more than an expedient thing, or that a new Nvidia CEO might act differently on that front. If I was in the AI or tech industry and thinking strategically, I would not want to make it look like the tech industry was rallying around Jensen Huang. That would substantially increase the chance and size of major political backlash. Jensen Huang Wants to Call It a Comeback Singularity Memes Highlights: they did the meme: He has discussed this potential comeback with allies. Tony Czuczka (Bloomberg): While Nvidia shares fell 12.7% last week, some shareholders expressed support for Jensen Huang, including his possible return to the company he helped turn into one of the world’s most valuable companies. One of those allies is Gavin Baker, calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement, including supporting his reinstatement now pending the investigation. Balaji of course is on the train as well, trying to vibe and threaten Jensen back into power in various ways and grasping at straws. As are Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick and over 170,000 signatories. They also arranged for a letter warning that ‘irreplaceable’ talent could be lost if Jensen Huang is not reinstated. There are always such warnings, and indeed some employees do leave when the CEO changes. That’s life. These people are even betting that this could happen. As in, see Polymarket, where people are buying Jensen Huang remaining as CEO at 16% (!?): No, sir. This is not going to happen. Even if the board were somehow willing to cave on this, and even if Trump says otherwise and is saying Huang ‘learned a big lesson,’ the rest of Washington is absolutely not going to allow Jensen Huang to run Nvidia. The board, knowing this and also for other very good reasons, is having none of it. Andrew Curran: CNBC is reporting that the NVIDIA board is focused on a national security investigation into Jensen Huang, and is not in discussions with him, or considering bringing him back as CEO. Robbie Whelan and Amrith Ramkumar (WSJ): Nvidia’s board of directors isn’t considering reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, despite a drumbeat of calls for his return from some investors and employees, according to a source familiar with the board’s thinking. This is the kind of thing that makes DC think that the tech industry is completely clueless and also hostile and dangerous. They flat out don’t get it. Or maybe I am the one who is wrong, because it is 2026 and literally nothing matters. There are plenty of out of line actions to go around. Donald Trump was out of line and being deeply silly to suggest a specific person, Tim Cook, take over Nvidia. Bessent was far less out of line, but still out of line, to tell Nvidia to pick an outsider and a ‘dramatic shakeup.’ Annmarie Hordern: Secretary Bessent to Fox: “I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” As Joe Weisenthal says, can you imagine if Elizabeth Warren was the one saying that? But also, the man has a point. If your company facilitates this level of blatantly illegal activity on matters vital to national security, I can see why you might need an outsider. OpenAI and Anthropic and SpaceX and Meta and so on have these different special governing structures, in theory or in practice, part of which is to make the CEO harder to fire. Matt Levine has fun going over the alternative versions of this crisis. I think he has too much fun. Sam Altman was able to be un-fired, but only because (among other reasons) the board was unable to explain its reasoning and the employees responded with an open revolt. In this case, the reasoning is very clear, and it is also clear to the national security state. The board might try to not fire Elon Musk in a similar situation. Good luck with that. If I was Jensen Huang, I would be less worried about trying to return as CEO and more worried about cooperation, and the potential civil and criminal implications, and hopefully also I would care about national security or even humans not all dying. On Interim CEO Kress I agree with Joe’s interpretation here of WSJ’s description of events. Joe Weisenthal: This WSJ story on Nvidia‘s interim CEO is interesting. The headline frames it around personality. A clash between Huang and Kress. But actually it seems like a fundamentals story. That there’s a sense of stress within the company about its growing leverage. Jensen Huang’s style was highly abrasive. I think the WSJ article was painting this disagreement into something that it was not, and that it does not provide much evidence of Jensen Huang’s central opinions about Kress. An Actual Attack on Jensen’s Character Pat McGovern: from jensen’s biographer ( @stephenwitt ) in today’s NYT Stephen Witt: Mr. Huang went to considerable lengths to cloak his arrogance. When I first met him in 2023, he and his handlers were pushing the idea that he was a humble man. In our conversations, Mr. Huang was constantly deflecting attention away from his success, always quick to assign credit to his employees and executive staff members. He also liked to glad-hand service people. He’d been a dishwasher himself once, a point he never let you forget. He loved visiting small, hole-in-the-wall restaurants and leaving extravagant tips. I’d met him for breakfast at Denny’s, and he tipped our waitress $1,000 in hundred-dollar bills. He didn’t make a show of it, either. I had to track her down to ask. Over time, though, I began to suspect that this was an act, one performed not for the observer, but to flatter himself. Austen Allred: If I were a billionaire I would quietly tip $1,000 all the time and I would get a lot of pleasure out of it. I just don’t understand how that makes someone arrogant. Yes, if you are quietly tipping waitresses $1,000 you are not doing it as an Effective Altruist. You are largely doing it because you feel great doing it. I don’t think it is an ‘act,’ even if it is largely a form of consumption. It’s exactly as Allred says, it is a happy thing to do. I’m all for it, even if one motivation of it is that it will inevitably leak. The part that matters is the second half, and given what I’ve seen on podcasts I have little doubt that Witt is accurate here: Stephen Witt: In truth, Mr. Huang was quite arrogant. He had little tolerance for disagreement and almost no capacity for open discourse. When you contradicted him, even over the most trivial matter, it was like lighting a fuse. Stick to your position and soon he exploded, screaming at you for your idiocy. A harangue from Mr. Huang could last an hour or more; his executive staff appeared genuinely afraid of him. Listening to their stories, I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from the movie “Whiplash.” Austen Allred: “We went to Denny’s and I later learned he tipped the waitress $1,000. He didn’t let anyone know that, I only learned after I tracked the waitress down and asked how big the tip was. I can only conclude from this that he was a very arrogant man masking his arrogance.” Huh? Zach Alberico: I can only conclude from this the biographer is the worst kind of randian villian. This kind of ‘cult of the great man’ reaction is understandable in the face of the whiplash here, but neglects that Witt claims very strong direct evidence. He’s not saying that the tip itself was the evidence of arrogance. We also have this article about Put-Downs, Parties and a ‘Royal Family.’ Neil Mehta: this story is nuts Anissa Gardizy, Robbie Whelan, Katherine Long and Hannah Critchfield (WSJ): The dressing downs Huang administered to employees, which one Nvidia executive described as “eviscerations,” had also become more frequent, according to people who have witnessed the episodes. He had one such blowup during a recent “e-staff” meeting, an early-morning gathering of his executive staff, according to people who were present. After Vladimir Troy, a senior executive, discussed delays to Nvidia’s data-center builds, Huang excoriated Troy in front of the group, using abusive language. “When Jensen does that, it is very painful. It’s crazy,” said one of the executives present. “He put Nvidia first, above any person.” Joe Weisenthal: A lot of people say this is very common behavior among CEOs. But I’ve read enough articles to know that all of this sounds like prevalent behavior among anyone with direct reports, in both the public and private sectors. I mean, yes, of course you put the company above any person. Or at least any person other than yourself. That’s how it works. Whole Mars Catalogue (quoting an article): People familiar with the matter say Jensen Huang’s “imperial control” extended to the Nvidia cafeteria, where he allegedly made employees try the brisket. “He kept saying ‘you have to try this,’” one source said. “Nobody felt they could say no.” And if the CEO tells you to try the brisket? You try the brisket. PoliMath: biographer on Jensen Huang: “I was reminded of the abusive music instructor from Whiplash” ok, but he was the hero of that movie Whiplash is a great movie. The instructor is, in my view, neither hero nor villain. He simply is who he is, as is the student. He is a man who chooses the pursuit of greatness and is willing to have you pay the price for it. You can decide whether he is right to do that. The same applies to this aspect of Jensen Huang, or many other founders. They are often highly not fun people to be around. This can lead to greatness. You can decide what to think about that. Solve for the New Equilibrium I see why Dean Ball is taking the contrary position, but I fear that he is wrong. Jeffrey Ladish (Palisade Research): How hard would be it be for a future swarm of AI agents to take down someone like Jensen by leaking information about an affair or two? People don’t understand how AI could take over without robots, often because they can’t model a well resourced, strategic adversary. Intelligence agency operations are a lower bound for what a strategic group of rogue agents could accomplish. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Quite hard, because by the time ai is good enough to autonomously perform that kind of intelligence collection, the capability will quickly diffuse broadly, many secrets of many people will have been exposed, and society will have recalibrated. Jeffrey Ladish (Palisade Research): Why do you think that it will defuse broadly? I’m guessing you’re assuming weak RSI only here? When anyone gets to strong RSI, I’d expect these capabilities to rapidly move beyond anything human society has or could adapt to. But even with ‘weak’ RSI, it seems quite plausible that one or several labs could have, or be had by, internal capabilities of this kind. Partially this is because I think the strong to weak spectrum is pretty spectrum-y, especially in worlds that don’t have a very fast foom, but I think you’d instead see an extremely steep slope of fairly smooth advances. But that would leave little time for either diffusion or adaptation, even if the capabilities are not yet strongly superhuman. The current situation is that many people, including very powerful people but also many ordinary people, have a bunch of secrets that could harm them quite a bit if weaponized. Often many of those secrets are not that hard to find. If you want to dig up dirt on someone, there is a good chance you can find it. If you are an intelligence agency, you can also create it by engineering the situation, including but not limited to honeypots, entrapment and scams, or of course you can also fabricate the information. There are also any number of pieces of true information (e.g. your banking password) that you would very much not want others to know, even if you are doing nothing wrong. Or perhaps rather than you ‘doing something wrong’ what is being leaked are things like business secrets and logistical information, or your home address. I think of this as analogous to cyber. Offense generally defeats defense under realistic conditions, because offense can concentrate firepower. You will not sufficiently harden defenses everywhere (which here would mean having no meaningful secrets) unless and until you expect to get hit for real. So Dean Ball’s adjustment probably only happens if you have anarchist-style or other groups out there trying to expose all the info like this on the regular, for the lulz or in principle or what not. But This Time They’ve Gone Too Far I do want to stand up for Jensen Huang in at least this small way: His plaque. Andrew Curran: The Jensen Huang commemorative plaque above the booth at the San Jose Denny’s where Jensen and his co-founders decided to start Nvidia has been removed. Erased… from existence. That action, in particular, is an outrage, assuming the story is true. This man earned that plaque. Let us not take away from Jensen Huang his thirty-three year history of building Nvidia. There would be no Nvidia, certainly not in anything like its present form, without the efforts of Jensen Huang. He has created trillions in value, most of which did not come from his dealings with China and those smuggling chips to China or allowing them remote access, or his hard lobbying, regulatory capture and technical evasions of export controls. This was mostly a company that builds great products. Respect. He is also responsible for his own downfall, and for choosing to sell so many chips to China when there was other demand for them, and for intentionally leaving Nvidia without an easy succession path. When we see the company decline in value by more than $570 billion in a week, that too is on him, not merely the lost opportunity from his leadership. Let us remember him for all of it.

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.content: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen, who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models, to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model, while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model. In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das, a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs. It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction. In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings. “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince. “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company: from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here, that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models, where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic, launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it!” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space, because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

items.title: Scoop up three great 4K Blu-ray movies for $33
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.content: A screenshot from the movie Sinners featuring Michael B. Jordan. | Image: Warner Bros. Gruv always keeps its proverbial fire hose of deals on movies running with a steady stream throughout the year, but the online seller operated by Universal Pictures is really letting it rip now ahead of Black Friday. The site has a page filled with 4K Blu-rays eligible for a “three for $33” promotion, and the catalog covers a lot of genres and time periods. There are Hitchcock films, cult classics, animated gems, and more recent titles included that deserve a spot on your shelf. If I had to pick three of my own, here’s what I’d go with: Batman: Mask of the Phantasm, Rear Window, and Sinners. Or, maybe I’d swap one for First Man because I can never get enough of its tense opening scene, or BlackkKlansman because it’s just so good. There’s a lot to like with the promo catalog. However, if you don’t mind spending a little more, Gruv has plenty more titles at $12.99 each, including newer releases. Several big box office films are here, from Obsession and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie to One Battle After Another, Weapons, and the fairly recent 4K Blu-ray launch of the Wachowski sisters’ Speed Racer, to name a handful of examples. You have no excuses not to load up holiday stockings with some fantastic goodies for the cinephile in your life (even if that’s you).

items.title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: Snowden Exposes NSA’s Lies
items.author: Josh Richman
items.content: By 2013, EFF had spent seven years arguing in court that the National Security Agency was sweeping up ordinary Americans’ communications, including through the secret room that whistleblower Mark Klein had exposed. The government would neither confirm nor deny it, and outside the courtroom the public seemed to have moved on. Then, in early June, documentary filmmaker Laura Poitras and journalist Glenn Greenwald mysteriously missed a Freedom of the Press Foundation board meeting at EFF’s offices. It turned out they were in Hong Kong, meeting an NSA contractor who had been secretly writing to Laura for months. His name was Edward Snowden, he had thousands of secret documents proving the government had in fact been spying on millions of Americans. When he subsequently revealed himself, a photo of him sitting behind his laptop – emblazoned with a big red EFF sticker – went worldwide. Welcome to the fourth episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was. %3Ciframe%20height%3D%2252px%22%20width%3D%22100%25%22%20frameborder%3D%22no%22%20scrolling%3D%22no%22%20seamless%3D%22%22%20src%3D%22https%3A%2F%2Fplayer.simplecast.com%2F21ba982d-0892-47e9-a638-36b5fae0e2d7%3Fdark%3Dtrue%26amp%3Bcolor%3D000000%22%20allow%3D%22autoplay%22%3E%3C%2Fiframe%3E Privacy info. This embed will serve content from simplecast.com (You can also find this episode on the Internet Archive and on YouTube.) In this episode, former EFF Executive Director Cindy Cohn talks with Laura Poitras about how she got to that historic moment, including her years of expertise in communicating via encrypted channels. Freedom of the Press Foundation Executive Director Trevor Timm – a former EFF activist – shares his recollection of the day the first Snowden story broke. For EFF and its clients in Jewel v. NSA, Snowden’s documents were proof of what the government had spent years refusing to confirm. As Cindy puts it, “We were struggling along in the mud, and we felt like somebody gave us wings.” It's the story of the lawyers who fought for your privacy, the government that lied about spying on you, and the whistleblower who blew it all wide open. The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so pick up your copy today! Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast. Jarrod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it. Corinne Ruff is our story editor. We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman. The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.

items.title: Inference engineering for software engineers
items.author: Gergely Orosz
items.content: A recent trend we’ve covered is of tech companies moving to open models to rein in AI spend: Uber cut its per-token costs by 50%, Pinterest by 90%, and even AT&T has achieved a 56% decrease. But how do you move from a frontier lab’s APIs to using open models? There are two options: “Bare metal:” With plenty of time and money, you can go “bare metal” and purchase a few dozen NVIDIA GPUs and use those AI supercomputers, like Revolut has done: running 56 separate B200 units itself to serve its inference needs. This is a lot of work to set it up, but after that, operational costs are as cheap as it gets. Inference provider: most companies contract with an inference provider that operates large fleets of GPUs, and makes it easy for customers to onboard and start using open models fast. Onboarding to an inference provider to run LLM workloads comes with challenges, such as dealing with tail latencies, worrying about cache hit rates, rate limits, and more. Inference engineering is a set of engineering practices that we believe is increasingly beneficial for software engineers to familiarize themselves with. To go deeper into this area, we’ve talked with three leading inference providers to learn more: Modal, Fireworks AI, and Baseten. Today, we cover: What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs? They have GPU infrastructure similar to frontier labs, don’t train their own frontier models and are experts at hosting open models. When to switch from frontier labs? The most common reasons are to reduce costs, have more control over latency, and to fine-tune AI models. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy. Use evals to find the right open model for your use case, evaluate vendors, and decide between multi-tenant API usage and dedicated GPUs. Stage #1: API replacement using a multi-tenant inference setup. The easiest way to onboard to an inference provider is to “swap” the API of a frontier lab to an API of an inference provider. But there may be latency problems and caching issues at high loads. Signs you’ve outgrown multi-tenant inference APIs. Hitting rate limits, performance consistency problems, and overpaying for usage are signs that it might be time to adopt dedicated GPUs. Stage #2: Configuring dedicated GPU nodes. With dedicated GPUs, you’ll need to get into the details: size of the model, interactivity versus throughput, KV cache sizing, failover options, and more. Speculative decoding. If there’s unused compute during the decode phase, you might consider a Speculator to further boost inference performance. As usual, we have no affiliation with vendors mentioned in this article, and have not been paid to mention any company. Special thanks to Richard Gong (Inference lead, Modal), Dmytro Dzhulgakov (cofounder and CTO, Fireworks), and Philip Kiely (Special Projects at Baseten) for sharing details about inference engineering challenges. 1. What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs? Inference providers are companies that sell access to LLMs which they run on users’ behalf. From the outside, this isn’t so different to what OpenAI and Anthropic offer: an API endpoint, ability to stream tokens, and pay based on token usage. But what makes inference providers different from frontier labs is the models running behind the endpoint: inference providers run open-weight models, whereas frontier labs train their own models. In this field, Modal, Fireworks, and Baseten each operate slightly different strategies: Modal sees itself as a cloud infrastructure provider that focuses on making its offering programmable via its SDKs. It natively supports inference services through its SDKs, but leans heavily on the open source ecosystem for running its inference workloads efficiently. Performance tweaks to its stack are merged upstream. In the words of Richard Gong, Inference Lead at Modal: “when you run code on Modal, you should be able to see all the code that’s running.” Fireworks positions itself as a provider for specialized AI workloads. Most of its business is in dedicated deployments, which often include fine-tuning and provision of latency guarantees. Much fine-tuning and post-training is available for self-service. Fireworks also offers forward-deployed researchers that can help with post-training custom models or components. Dmytro Dzhulgakov, Fireworks’ CTO, says: “our tagline is specialized intelligence, which means we will tune everything from model to infrastructure for your particular use case.” Baseten describes itself as an all-in-one place to build agents. It starts with the basic infrastructure layer with uptime guarantees, flexible commercial terms, without vendor lock-in. Baseten builds additional layers for building agentic workloads on top of its inference platform. These additional layers include sandboxes, governance services, and self-serving, post-training functionality. To customers, inference providers offer LLM APIs that can be used as drop-in replacements for frontier labs’ APIs. However, inference providers are not the same, as suggested above: Inference providers don’t pre-train their own foundational models. A single pre-training run for frontier-level LLMs can cost millions of dollars, and only hyperscalers and specialized frontier labs can afford it. Inference providers run post-training on open-weight models because it’s significantly cheaper. Competitive pricing. The main business of inference providers is offering open-weight models at competitive rates. Dedicated hardware. A big part of the appeal of inference providers is the ability to have dedicated hardware for users to interact with vendors on the infrastructure layer. Efficiency & customization. Inference providers offer similar commoditized open models, and compete heavily on efficiency and customization services. As an example of efficiency, Fireworks announced its Ember-1 model in September 2026, that is post-trained on the Kimi K3 foundation, delivering a similar quality level but with 40% fewer reasoning tokens consumed. Consuming far fewer reasoning tokens gives Fireworks an edge on cost compared to a vanilla Kimi K3 model. In general, frontier labs have poor uptime, and this helps inference vendors win market share. API Uptime provided by frontier labs isn’t at the levels expected of modern cloud providers: currently, the self-declared uptime of Anthropic is 99.5%, and for OpenAI it’s 99.97% for API, and 99.2% for ChatGPT. These numbers are well below the four nines (99.99%+) uptime expected of cloud providers – which is something that a vendor like AWS is known to uphold. Frontier labs’ API uptime. Sources: OpenAI, Anthropic. Imagine you’re a developer aiming to provide a 99.99% uptime guarantee for your application; you can’t rely on a single frontier LLM provider for the service’s critical path. But in the graphs above, degraded performance slots aren’t counted as downtime. As all these APIs are multi-tenant, it means that performance degradations will naturally hit some tenants – with no way to be aware of the degradation, or do anything about it. Reliability is an ongoing concern with the LLMs of frontier providers and inference providers. Even though many inference vendors offer higher reliability guarantees than frontier models, inference providers can also go down, too. For companies that use inference providers, it’s common to use an LLM gateway with fallback logic to another provider – or to a frontier API. We explored this in a deepdive with Ramp, whose LLM router project started with this exact problem statement. 2. When to switch from frontier labs? Moving from frontier AI labs to an independent inference provider is often driven by three factors: cost, control, and the need for more customization. Most common reason: cost Many companies start considering inference providers because they have pressing cost concerns. In many cases, a frontier model is more capable than necessary for most requests, meaning a “dumber” model is just as good for simpler tasks – and nobody would notice the difference! In such cases, it’s a “no-brainer” for an engineering team to choose to route some requests to a cheaper model hosted by an inference provider. “Smart routing” is an obvious way to cut costs. An LLM router – the “smart router” – is prompt-aware and can route an LLM request to the most cost-efficient provider that can solve the request. This is an approach that fuelled Uber’s ~50% cut in per-token costs this summer. Providers offer OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API endpoints, so switching providers is trivial. All that is needed is to point your app at the new endpoint operated by a “smart router.” But how to decide which model to serve? Generic benchmarks are often insufficient because they usually do not fully represent a team’s traffic patterns. Most inference providers ask for prompt samples or eval sets in order to gauge which model best serves a customer’s use case. The experience of using a new LLM endpoint resembles using APIs provided by frontier labs, while API calls are still charged per token, and response time SLAs generally don’t exist. More control over latency When you use a frontier lab’s endpoint, there is little control over operational issues like response latency and model availability. Opting for a dedicated setup with an inference provider offers full control over both: Latency: model response times are more predictable because the app has dedicated capacity that can scale by usage. Model availability: Engineers can run the model of their choosing on their dedicated GPUs and keep operating it as long as needed, avoiding the risk of a frontier lab changing models from one day to the next. Fine-tuning model quality: customization When an inference stack runs on dedicated hardware with open source models, it’s possible to work with inference providers to finetune a model’s quality as required, which optimizes latency or throughput performance. Richard Gong of Modal says that around 10% of their customers go this far, suggesting that customization is for “power users”. Fine-tuning a model’s quality is typical in two scenarios: Tweaking a smaller model: achieving a similar level of quality with a smaller model, with fewer parameters. This performance gain is achieved via performance tweaks not possible with off-the-shelf models. Inference providers allow you to post-train a smaller model for your specific use case. A post-trained small model can then outperform the original model in those specialized scenarios. Fine tuning for niche use cases. Improving quality when general purpose models aren’t good enough, often because the data isn’t publicly available. For example, projects in the legal and medical sectors tend to benefit from this, according to the Fireworks team. 3. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy Most inference providers offer the exact same models to run, and the differences lie in model performance and quality. For example, model quality can differ by default context length, and some providers cap this to below what the model supports. There’s also quantization to consider, where a model’s weights are compressed to a lower numerical precision, or default temperature aka controlling how random the output is. Here’s a practical approach for selecting a provider: Model: Choose an AI model to switch to Provider: pick an inference provider to host the model, based on model quality, performance, and cost Deployment model: decide whether to use a multi-tenant service, or to move to dedicated GPU nodes Choosing a model The most obvious way to decide which model to use is to run an eval set against the various model options. In the latest episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, Microsoft’s CEO Satya Nadella argues that private evals shall be a big component of tech companies’ intellectual property (IP) in the future. He says: “Public benchmarks are great, but your private evals will matter more: you need your own eval for the outcome that matters to you. Then you look at performance across all these models and continuously optimize. Our customers start with a frontier model, then say: ‘I’ve got all those traces. This is a deterministic workflow, so I don’t need the next big model drop. I want to optimize the cost.’ They drop in [another] model, use the traces to fine-tune it – and there you have it.” An example of public benchmarks is from Artificial Analysis that maintains an eval set to compare costs for generic tasks across different models. Here are the average costs per task, broken down by model: Artificial Analysis Cost Per Intelligence Index Task. Source: Artificial Analysis Let’s say you build an app on top of Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 model, costing $5.46 on average per task in the index. If Kimi K3 is sufficient for this use case, then that model is ~60% cheaper to run at only $2.00 per task. Note that the cost comparison here is per-task, not per-token. This makes sense because different models require different numbers of tokens to complete a task, which makes it harder to compare model costs without your own private evals! Having said that, deciding whether a model is good enough requires more than just looking at public benchmark results. Ideally, there’s an eval set to compare models with. In the absence of that, running an A/B experiment is a good alternative. For example, if you want to switch agentic coding workflows to an inference provider, you could simply let some engineers use the new model and give feedback on the results. Choosing a provider All providers tweak open models to squeeze out more performance without degrading quality too much. Therefore, model outputs and quality vary among providers. A useful tool for comparing providers’ model accuracy is Artificial Analysis’ endpoint accuracy index. This is a score that benchmarks results from various inference providers against its own, self-hosted version. An index value of 100% means the provider’s results are the same as Artificial Analysis’ own hosted model. Kimi K3 endpoint accuracy across various providers. Source: Artificial Analysis Endpoint accuracy is broadly similar and the scores of providers range from 93% to 102%. The variance comes from performance and quality tweaks that inference providers make to their versions of open models. Since LLMs are non-deterministic, this measurement has a 95% confidence interval – which adds another layer of complexity to evaluation. Minor score differences are considered within the same level as Artificial Analysis’ reference model, hence the green coloring of bars that are technically below 100%. Deployment model: multi-tenant or dedicated? All providers’ offerings include a multi-tenant API, as well as dedicated GPUs to run LLMs. This deployment progression is typically a graduation path: most deployments start as drop-in API replacements of frontier labs’ APIs, and as usage grows they start switching to dedicated infrastructure. When switching to an open model hosted by an inference provider, the per-token cost decreases. However, you are still running in a multi-tenant environment, which comes with similar performance bottlenecks, like when using the API endpoint of a frontier model. The difference is that with an inference provider, you can migrate to a dedicated hosting environment and have full control over a deployment’s performance. Having your own deployment (controlling the GPUs with the inference provider) makes it possible to fine-tune a model’s quality with techniques such as post-training. Typical graduation path from multi-tenant API to dedicated GPUs The most typical path for a startup using LLMs: Use a frontier lab’s API endpoints Move over to using an open model, using the API endpoint of an inference provider Rent dedicated GPUs from the inference provider Three-stage graduation path for inference provider users Moving to an inference provider is usually coupled with achieving some kind of product-market fit. All three inference providers we spoke with told us that by the time a customer signs up by getting to “stage 1” (see below), their product has gained traction in the market. Per-token costs only become important with non-trivial levels of user activity. “Stage 2” with dedicated GPUs is a level that implies significant budget commitments, a more mature product, and large-scale usage. Getting inference capacity: this can be tricky, given the global GPU shortage! We previously covered how there’s a CPU shortage inside cloud providers – and so there should be no surprise that there’s an even more pressing GPU shortage. Even large inference providers are having a hard time getting all the GPUs they need. The inference providers we talked with all run on top of several cloud providers – plus some also manage their own bare metal – exactly to get as much capacity as they can. Getting access to more GPUs justifies the added operational complexity from running in multiple clouds. Being able to quickly onboard new cloud providers that have spare capacity is becoming a key differentiator in the industry. If you need dedicated GPUs, know that it will probably be expensive. Scarce capacity is one of the reasons why getting a dedicated setup typically requires long-term budget commitments upfront. To put it simply: you’ll need to pay a larger amount, and commit for paying for those GPUs on a longer timeframe. 4. Stage #1: API replacement, using a multi-tenant inference setup For teams with hefty LLM bills, the easiest way to decrease cost is to replace frontier labs’ models in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, with a frontier-level open model. Looking at data from OpenCode and OpenRouter, the current most popular choices of engineering teams for this include DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and others including Kimi K3.1 Pro. The easiest way to carry out a replacement is to point an application to an API provided by the inference provider. In practice, this means using a multi-tenant API where other customers will be hitting the same endpoint, similar to using an API endpoint from a frontier lab. At first, everything will be great, but then you may come across problems of time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency, caching-related costs, and latency issues. These are also problems of using APIs from frontier labs, the difference being that with inference providers, there’s the option of solving most of them by moving over to a dedicated deployment. Latency problems: TTFT, inference time, user-experienced latency Time-to-first-token is a measure of how long it takes from the moment a request hits the LLM API, to when the client starts receiving the first tokens. The distribution of TTFT latencies has a long tail: Illustrative shape of TTFT latency distribution. Source: Baseten. A long right tail means that a significant proportion of requests have double the median latency or longer. So, when measuring latencies, the p95/p99 latencies are just as important as p50 latencies. TTFT can be measured in two places: Inference time: provider-instrumented TTFT shows the pure inference time. Some providers expose this metric to customers on dashboards, while some include it in their responses. Frontier labs typically do neither. User-experienced latency: client-instrumented TTFT shows the full user-experienced latency, including things like network transport, or the TLS handshake. Server-side inference is just one part of the overall time that an app’s user spends awaiting a response. To achieve truly fast p95 times for user latency, it’s best to consider optimizations like connection pooling on the LLM API consumer side. When serving LLM APIs on shared infrastructure, inference providers run many copies of the LLM inference engine that serves customer requests. A single inference engine can serve multiple requests concurrently. A new replica is created when the number of concurrent requests exceeds the current replica capacity. Scaling of replicas is one reason why inference-only TTFT latencies vary so much. Other reasons why TTFT can vary: ‘Noisy neighbour’ effects: a request is batched with another request that’s more expensive to process, so it takes longer than if the request was in a batch with a similar request. Cold start: happens when a request is waiting in a queue because there is no capacity in existing replicas. The inference provider is creating new replicas but this isn’t instantaneous, so a request has to wait until the new replica becomes available (until the new replica starts up, from a “cold”, offline state). Cold cache: when sending a large request for the first time, it may end up on a replica without the relevant KV cache loaded (the cache is “cold” – which is the opposite of “hot cache” when the KV cache is already populated). An inference provider will typically try to keep requests sticky to the same replica because that keeps replica’s KV cache hot. Sometimes, this isn’t possible because your cache expired, or it landed on the replica that doesn’t have the relevant KV cache. KV cache then has to either be copied from cold storage if available, or if it’s not, fully processed before the first token can be generated. Prompt cache utilization is observable and actionable by engineers building on LLM APIs. You can get prompt cache utilization metrics from the response of the OpenAI completions API. Building your apps to effectively exploit prompt cache is a key technique in improving app performance, so it’s worth taking a closer look. Caching issues: cost and latency Most major LLM API endpoints today are stateless REST APIs, inspired by OpenAI’s chat completions API. LLM endpoints are stateless, which creates problems because most LLM use cases are stateful. Dmytro Dzhulgakov, cofounder and CTO at Fireworks calls the decision to make the API stateless “the original sin” because while the client app behaves like it’s talking to a stateless API, the burden is on the provider to ensure efficient caching mechanisms in a distributed environment. Here’s an example to illustrate the problems that stateless APIs cause: an app with user’s inputs, LLM prompts, and the agentic context layer: Read more
