items.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
items.content: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io: Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README. I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML. This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite. Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: This should work for every other Python app, too Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs. C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026. One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden. I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem. For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers Tags: javascript, projects, python, urls, datasette, webassembly, service-workers, pyodide, datasette-lite

items.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
items.author: Ryan Whitwam
items.content: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app. The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road. As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You'll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It's under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity. Read full article Comments

It all started in Switzerland, according to a source familiar with the outage. Exchange Online servers that power Outlook started to fall offline. items.title: Engineering AI Discover
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline. This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way. Why an intelligence layer? Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer. The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design: Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next. System Architecture When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor. The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later. A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails. Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served. The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code. Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system. System Architecture Diagram Key Decisions Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us. 1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs. This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own. 2. Make existing systems composable Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future. Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans. In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste. 3. Plan first, then execute To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs. Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan. This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one. 4. Stay model and capability agnostic The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM. That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change. Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release. Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment. 5. Make page generation asynchronous Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving. Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it. Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen. Async Sequence Diagram 6. Enforce safety in code Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs. For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection. Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay. Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product. 7. Remember what members tell us A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post. In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context. The member holds the remote In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design. The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else. Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards. What’s next It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind. We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions: How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems. What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests. Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately. This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix. Acknowledgements We would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work. items.title: Four Continents, Four New AWS Heroes: Closing Out 2026
items.author: Taylor Jacobsen
items.content: As AWS re:Invent is around the corner, we’re proud to recognize a new group of AWS Heroes. Every Hero finds their own way to give back, whether through sharing what they know, bringing people together, or building tools that help others succeed. What they have in common is a genuine commitment to supporting the builders around them learn, grow, and lead. Let us take a moment to meet them! Andres Moreno – El Paso, United States Serverless Hero Andres Moreno leads the Cloud del Norte AWS User Group and is a former AWS Community Builder. On his blog, And More Dev, and at conferences and community events, he explains serverless, cloud native architectures, generative AI, and agentic systems in ways that make new technology easier to try. Andres puts special energy into supporting builders across Latin America and helping them explore what’s possible on AWS. Geethika Guruge – Auckland, New Zealand Community Hero Geethika Guruge is a Principal Consultant at Mantel Group whose work spans serverless, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, and agentic AI. Geethika has shared real lessons from building agentic applications and leading large migration and modernization programs at AWS re:Invent, AWS Summits, and AWS Community Days. At home in Auckland, Geethika organizes local AWS meetups that encourage grassroots innovation and mentors the next generation of cloud architects and leaders. Jéssica Cristina Coelho – Belo Horizonte, Brazil Data Hero Jéssica Cristina Coelho is a Database Reliability Engineer and a former AWS Community Builder with more than 15 years of experience in databases, cloud, and data engineering. She leads the AWS User Group in Minas Gerais, hosts DataTalks Brasil, teaches MBA courses, and supports Women in Cloud, DevOpsDays, and AWS Community Day events. She speaks at events such as AWS Summit São Paulo and Web Summit Rio on database modernization and generative AI. At AWS re:Invent 2025, she was recognized as a LATAM Diversity & Inclusion Champion. Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka – Tokyo, Japan DevTools Hero Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka is an AWS CDK Top Contributor and Trusted CDK Community Reviewer. With 200 merged pull requests, he ranks 18th among more than 1,700 contributors. He has reviewed more than 120 pull requests, has been involved in about 2% of all CDK commits, and has published 10 construct libraries, along with tools such as cfn idle cost. Through talks at JAWS DAYS and CDK Conference Japan and through hands on contribution workshops, he helps more developers in Japan start contributing to open source.
